topic: Jade Spirit Game - Roblox Build Package.docx
content:
JADE SPIRIT
Shrine of the Blooming Grove


Cover — JADE SPIRIT: Oakley, the headless green jade skeleton in her pink and brown ghillie, the Golden Dragon Rifle in her hands, defending the floating island and its Giant Pink Crystal Cherry Blossom Tree from the zombie horde below — the whole game in one frame: home above, the apocalypse below, and the sniper between.
A complete Roblox build package — game design, avatar & skin spec, step-by-step Studio build, paste-ready Luau code, and a publishing checklist.
Game Design  •  Studio Build  •  Luau Code  •  Publishing Checklist

Contents
Build in order the first time: Chapters 1–14 are the core game, Chapters 28–53 are its advanced systems and business layer; Chapter 45 is the master interlock, Chapter 49 the measurement ledger. Chapter numbers are the locators throughout — every cross-reference in this package, in prose and in code, resolves to a chapter in this list.

Chapters 15–27 are not missing: that numbering belonged to an earlier draft, in which the systems now consolidated into Chapters 3, 4, 6, and 28–44 carried their own numbers. The code comments still carry a few of those old numbers; Chapter 45 includes the concordance that maps each one to its current chapter, so no reference is left dangling.




START HERE — from your account, on your PC, to a published game
This is the build path, on a PC, in order. Everything else in this package is reference for one of these steps — each step names its chapter, and no step needs anything that is not in this document or free from Roblox. Work top to bottom; a step is done when its check line passes. If you only have an evening, Steps 1–5 give you a playable Grove; the systems after that are additive in order and none of them rewrites an earlier step.

Step 7 — the paste points: two UserIds and the Dashboard IDs
The whole package has exactly 49 fields you must fill with your own numbers. Nothing else is missing, anywhere: every other value in every script is finished. The fields are of two kinds. USERIDs identify people and never change. DASHBOARD IDs identify passes and products you create in Steps 8–9 and are created by you, for free, in the Creator Dashboard. A field left at 0 is not an error — it disables exactly its own item, and each register row says what stays dark until it is filled.
Finding a UserId (do this for Oakley's account and for her brother's account, once each): on the PC, log in at roblox.com AS THAT ACCOUNT, open the profile page, and read the number in the address bar — roblox.com/users/<NUMBER>/profile. That number is the UserId. It is permanent, it is not the username, and it is not the display name: if the number came from anywhere except that address bar, do not use it. Write both numbers here once, on paper if you like: Oakley's UserId (she is the Bloom twin, and the exclusive skeleton) and her brother's UserId (he is the Shadow/Guardian twin). Every row below that says 'Oakley's' takes the first number; every row that says 'his / the brother's' takes the second — the SAME two numbers in all 12 places. Your own UserId, Taylor, appears in NO row: you are the game's owner, Roblox identifies you by your login (the game's CreatorId is your UserId), and nothing in any script needs your number typed in. If any future script asks for an 'owner ID', the answer is yours — and it should read it from the game, not from a paste.


One optional extra, not counted in the 49: Script 42's POSES table holds eight pose AnimationIds, all shipped at 0. They are content, not setup — a pose with no AnimationId is skipped safely (Chapter 33), and the game is complete without them. If you later upload your own pose animations in the Creator Dashboard, paste their IDs there; nothing else changes.
Steps 8–10, to finish the path: (8) CREATE THE PASSES AND PRODUCTS — in Creator Hub → your experience → Monetization, create every item in the register above at its chapter's price, and paste each ID the moment it is created, row by row. Nothing can be bought before this step and everything works without it except the shops. Ticket IDs live in Script 49's CONFIG and skin IDs in Script 51's SKINS table (the registers above); Script 10's receipt handler routes each completed purchase to its grant automatically — there is nothing to wire by hand. (9) TEST AS A PLAYER, NOT AS THE OWNER — Chapter 11's protocol, on a second, free account (your own account owns the game, so it can see and do things a player cannot; never judge the player experience from it): the First Choice, the counts, the gates, a Vault purchase with the test account, a Colosseum ticket, and — logged in as Oakley's account — the shrine toggle that must work for her and must NOT appear for the test account (Chapter 9's troubleshooting if it does). Also run Chapter 14's exploit protocol once, in a private server, before anyone else is invited. (10) PUBLISH — Chapter 12's checklist, in order: game settings, icon and thumbnails (Chapter 10's plan; the cover art of this package is the launch thumbnail's base), audience and chat settings for a younger-players-first game, then Game Settings → Permissions → Public. The checklist's last box is the game, live and discoverable, under your own account — and Step 9's test account finding it in search is the proof.

1  The characters — the Twin Guardians
The guardians are TWINS — brother and sister, one silhouette in two mirrored palettes. She is pink and jade; he is white and violet. Same wood armor, same long wood spear, same single crystal wing — on mirrored sides. Two design signatures read instantly in a thumbnail, in a crowd of avatars, and at a distance across a map — which is exactly what a Roblox game needs. The two reference portraits in this chapter are the CANONICAL designs: every spec, build step, and piece of art direction in this package matches them exactly.

Their glowing eyes set the accents: pink crystal is her spirit energy, violet crystal is his. In the game, anything pink or violet is worth chasing — shards, blooms, trails, and the final arena. Anything thorny and grey is a spirit that needs freeing, never an enemy to destroy. That one rule keeps the whole game kind, readable, and true to both twins.
Their story — the core myth
Before there were Keepers, there was the Tree. The Great Blossom Tree grew where the world's first spring broke through crystal stone, and it grew the way crystal grows — slowly, in light — until its trunk was living crystal and its blossom never fell. Everything in the Grove is the Tree keeping a promise: that nothing here is ever lost, only sleeping. The village grew in its shade, the statue was carved facing it, and the first guardian gave her life to its keeping.
She is the heart of the myth: the First Guardian, whose form — the Headless Jade Spirit of Chapter 9 — still walks the Grove in legend. When the Thorn Sleep first crept in, a grey drowsiness that wraps spirits in thorn and puts them to sleep where they stand, she gave the Tree the one thing the Sleep could not take: her head, her crown, her name — offered freely, so the Tree would always know a guardian's face and the Sleep would never find a head to crown itself with. That is why she is headless. She did not lose her head in battle; she spent it, the way a keeper spends everything, on the Grove. Her pink bow floats where her head would be, because she was laughing when she made the trade, and the Grove remembers.
Her company were not so lucky, and they are the game's tragedy, not its target practice. The keepers who followed her tried to hold the whole Grove awake by will alone, and the Sleep took them standing — wrapped in husks of thorn and wood, asleep inside their own armor. Those are the Thorn Husks: sleeping spirits, freed by cracking the husk gently, never by harm. But a few slept too long and too deep, down in the Hollow where no blossom light reaches, and the Sleep wore their shapes down to the crystal itself and set them walking — the Hollow skeletons, thorn-bound keepers of pure crystal bone, drifting always toward the Tree's light because some part of them still remembers the watch. The Tree's crystal calls to the crystal in them. That is why the waves always come for the Tree. Players do not destroy them. Players hold the line, free what can be freed, and keep the Tree, the village, and the statue standing until dawn. Every enemy in this game was a guardian first. That is the rule the whole design obeys.
The twins are the watch now. A sister who walks the light between the trees and a brother who walks the violet dark beneath them, each carrying one half of the Twin Spear Pack — two long spears forged as a pair from one great branch of the Tree itself, hers tipped with jade crystal, his with violet. And every guardian, the twins first of all, carries their power in two forms: the Susanoo, the giant spectral guardian who stands around them — and the Daemon pet, that same guardian condensed into a living crystal bear who walks beside them, carries them, and flies with them. One being, two states; a spear in the hand and a bear at the side. Players are the twins' apprentices — the Bloom Keepers — learning to do the same: thrust, free, protect, and keep the Tree blooming.

The brother: the second Twin Guardian, canonical design. White spiky crown hair, purple crystal mask and horns, glowing violet eyes, pale violet glowing hands, ONE violet crystal wing on his right side, the same dark wood armor, and his Twin Spear — a long wood shaft with a violet crystal tip and gold accents. Build him from the same steps as his sister (Chapter 5) — only the palette and the wing side change.

2  The game at a glance
Jade Spirit is three games braided into one place, so different kids find different reasons to stay: explorers roam the Grove and do quests, jumpers climb the Sky Obby, and battlers clear the Crystal Arena together. Friends in the same server drift between all three and meet at the shrine.

The 60-second first impression
The core loadout — a weapon and a Daemon
Every player, from before their first minute in the Grove, has exactly two things, and the whole game is built around the pair — chosen, not given. A WEAPON, chosen FIRST, at the Threshold, before the tutorial and before World 1 itself (Chapter 34): one of the four starters — spear, katana, scythe, or hammer — its style, material, and quartz designed at the Spirit Workbench. And a COMPANION: their weapon's other self, which wakes as a BRANCH of the World Tree, grows into a living creature (sprite, fox, serpent, or bear cub — one per weapon, pink and brown), transforms into the weapon itself, and at guardian scale is their DAEMON — rideable, flyable, their condensed Susanoo (Chapter 32). Weapon strikes earn the counts; the companion and Daemon turn those strikes into movement and combos. Nothing else is required to play, and nothing sold ever replaces either half of the kit. Weapon + wings are the atomic design units underneath both halves — the weapon is designed, the wings are designed (Chapter 35), and the Susanoo and the Daemon are those same designs, manifested at two sizes (Chapters 28 and 30).
A new player's first sight is not the Grove — it is the Threshold (Chapter 34): four wooden stands under the World Tree's branch, four cards, one choice. They choose their weapon; the gate opens; a branch of the Tree lowers beside them; and in the Root Plaza, in front of everyone, the branch grows into their companion. Only then does the familiar sequence begin: the Jade Spirit NPC waves from the shrine steps, the first Sakura Shard spins three steps ahead, and in under a minute they have moved, collected, talked, and accepted their first quest — free three Thorn Husks. That order is deliberate: choice, companion, then the Grove — and no menus, shops, or pop-ups anywhere in it.

Concept art — a street of the floating island hometown (World 1): jade torii gate, shrine, bamboo, sakura trees, pink crystal clusters, lantern bridge, and the koi pond — one neighborhood of the island in the sky (full island view in Chapter 3). It is also your thumbnail reference.
3  Core loop, worlds, and quests
The core loop, in one line: explore → collect shards → free husks → earn blooms → unlock the next zone → dress the part → do it again with friends, faster and prettier.
World 1 — Cherry Blossom Japan: HOME
World 1 is not a level. It is HOME — and home FLOATS. The whole world is a FLOATING ISLAND in the sky: a Japanese-themed safe hometown built in rings on the island's green top around one thing — the Giant Crystal World Tree, a massive pink crystal cherry blossom tree whose trunk is living crystal, whose canopy spreads over the whole town, and whose crown dominates the skyline from every street, garden, and rooftop on the island. Traditional Japanese aesthetic throughout — pagodas, torii gates, wooden houses with dark tiled roofs, shrine roofs, stone lanterns, zen gardens, koi ponds, bamboo groves, sakura petals falling like slow snow — and all of it in the Tree's pink light. Waterfalls pour off the island's rocky edge and fall into the clouds below; the island's underside tapers to a rock point the Tree's roots grip from above (Chapter 39). And below the clouds, far below, is the zombie apocalypse (Chapters 3 & 41): the island floats ABOVE the danger — the safe zone is literally above the apocalypse, and every keeper at the island's rim can look down and see why the gates matter. This is the starting world: where players spawn, learn the game, customize, build, shop, socialize, prepare, and rest. The Tree stands here protected, at peace, and nothing in this world can hurt it or anyone in it.

Concept art — World 1, the floating island hometown: the Giant Pink Crystal Cherry Blossom Tree at the center of the island, pink crystal growing through its trunk and crown, blossom canopy over the town; pagodas, torii gates, wooden houses, stone lanterns, and smaller sakura in rings around it on the island's green top; waterfalls falling off the island's rocky underside into the clouds below — and below the clouds, out of frame, the apocalypse. Build toward this picture — if the Tree does not dominate the island's skyline, it is not big enough.

The rules of home — no PvP, no combat

Layout — rings around the Tree
Build World 1 as concentric rings on the flat, walkable top of the floating island, every street a sightline to the Tree. The island itself is built first (Chapter 41's sky-copy rule in reverse — this one is the original): a green-topped rock island about 700 studs across, its underside tapering to a point about 160 studs below the town, waterfalls (animated texture planes, Chapter 39's petal rule applies: cheap, pretty, no physics) falling from the rim streams into open sky. The rim is a place, not an edge case: a lantern-lit rim path circles the whole town where keepers look DOWN — through parting clouds at the grey valley of the apocalypse (Chapter 41) — and across at the Sky Obby's first platforms. A new player should be able to navigate by one rule from their first minute: walk toward the Tree to reach the middle of everything, walk away from it to reach homes and gates. Scatter 30 Sakura Shards and 5 hidden Crystal Blooms across the rings as the exploration layer — hidden means behind the shrine, under the lantern bridge, in the pagoda’s shadow, in the zen garden’s stones, and up the bamboo climb.

The Giant Crystal World Tree — the anchor
Spec the Tree like a character, because it is one. Trunk: twisted living wood grown around a core of glowing pink crystal, crystal clusters bursting through the bark at the roots, the fork, and the crown — Glass and Neon pink crystal in the Chapter 5 palette, lit from inside so the Tree is the world’s lamp at night. Canopy: blossom at a scale no ordinary sakura attempts — it roofs the Root Plaza completely and shades Ring 1, with petal-fall particles drifting down over the plaza at all hours. Roots: surface roots big enough to walk on, forming the plaza’s natural benches and the offering circle’s edge. Scale rule: from the Grand Torii at the edge of the world, the Tree fills the view over the rooftops; from any Ring 3 plot, its crown is still the tallest thing in the sky. If a pagoda competes with it, shrink the pagoda.
How the Tree anchors play, not just the view: offerings — keepers thrust at the Tree inside the 16-stud offering range and every counted thrust advances the shared global milestones (First Bloom, Blossom Legend, Eternal Spring, Script 13) in full view of the plaza; navigation — every signpost in World 1 is written as a direction from the Tree (Shrine Quarter: Tree-side; Plots: Outer Ring), so nobody is ever lost, only at a distance from the Tree; gatherings — events, group-ups, and photo calls happen at the Root Plaza by default, because it is the one place every player can find without a map; and story — the Statue faces it, the shrine serves it, the First Guardian gave her head to its roots (Chapter 1), and Oakley’s one rare form is its keeper (Chapter 9). The Tree is the reason the village exists, stated in stone, wood, and crystal on every street.
Landmarks — what to build, in build order

NPCs — the people of home

Tutorial flow — the first session, all at home
The whole tutorial happens inside the sanctuary, at walking pace, with the Tree in view the entire time. Nothing attacks, nothing times out, and a player can stop at any step and just live in the village — the tutorial resumes at the quest board. Combat is taught as a purpose here and practiced on straw in the Training Yard; the first real husk is beyond the gates, when the player chooses it.

Building plots — World 1 is a build world
Ring 3’s Building Plots are the home layer: a register of flat, lantern-lit plots around the outer ring, each claimed at the Plot Warden’s board and released back when a keeper moves on. On their own plot a keeper builds a home and a garden — house shells, fences, lanterns, sakura and bamboo planting, crystal pieces, a Daemon resting spot, a photo corner — placed from the build catalogue the Thrust Shop stocks with seeds, cosmetics, and garden plots (Scripts 13 + 18: spending Spend Balance only, Lifetime never moves). Plots are sanctuary ground in every rule that matters: no one can damage, edit, or enter-build on another keeper’s plot, weapons stay at rest on every plot, and a plot is a place to show friends, not a base to defend — there is nothing to defend it from, at home. Keep plot builds inside the village palette (wood, stone, bamboo, sakura, crystal) so Ring 3 still reads as one village from the pagoda balcony.
Social spaces and rest — why players stay
Home earns its playtime socially. The Root Plaza is the default hangout — benches on the roots, the milestone blooms as server-wide events, the leaderboard as conversation. The Tea House takes groups and roleplay; the Zen Garden takes two friends and quiet; the Koi Pond bridge and Pagoda steps are the photo stages; the Daemon Garden is where partners are compared, fed, and admired. Rest here is a designed state, not an absence of play: kimonos on (Chapter 31), spears stowed, Daemons dozing in the garden, petals falling. A session that never leaves World 1 — customize, build, shop, chat, offer at the Tree, rest — is a complete session by design, and for the youngest keepers it may be the whole game for weeks. That is a feature: the sanctuary is the retention engine, and the gates will still be there when they are ready.
Prepare, depart, return — the home loop
Every adventure in the other worlds is bookended by home — and home is UP. Prepare: change loadout and look at the Workbench Hall, swap kimono for armor, feed the Daemon, check the quest board, group up at the plaza, take the Gate Keeper’s briefing. Depart: walk through a rim gate and pick the world in the selection UI (Chapter 40) — the Sky Obby for climbing, the Crystal Arena for co-op husk-freeing, the apocalypse valley far below for the zombie waves and the hill (Chapters 41–42). Return: every world's gate opens the same UI with HOME first, and you rise back up to the island, where rewards are spent — shards and blooms at Market Row, thrust counts at the Thrust Shop, designs at the Workbench, pride at the garden fence. The Tree never leaves the center of that loop, because it never leaves the center of the world: it is the last thing a keeper sees through the gate light, and the first thing they see coming home.
World 2 — The Sky Obby
Floating wood platforms above the clouds, joined by rope bridges, golden rings, and one rainbow slide as the reward for the hardest stretch. Twelve jade checkpoints (Checkpoint_1 to Checkpoint_12) save progress permanently through the code in Chapter 8, so a player can leave mid-climb and resume tomorrow. Falling respawns at the last checkpoint — never at the start.

Concept art — World 2, the Sky Obby: wood platforms, a glowing jade checkpoint, golden rings, the rainbow slide, and sakura petals on the wind. The signs in this concept are world signage, painted on boards in Studio.
World 3 — The Crystal Arena
A round floating arena ringed with giant pink crystals. Waves of sleepy Thorn Husks wander in; a full server frees a wave together in about three minutes. Clearing a wave rains shards and spawns one Crystal Bloom in the center. There is no player-versus-player combat anywhere in this game — the arena is cooperative, and that is a feature to advertise, not a missing mode.

Concept art — World 3, the Crystal Arena: floating islands, rope bridges, pink crystal ring, jade crystal outcrops, and Daemon pets. The pink swirl is a Bloom Thrust's petal ring made visible.
Beyond the gates — the zombie apocalypse
The world has one law, and every keeper learns it at the island's rim, looking down: ABOVE IS PARADISE, BELOW IS THE APOCALYPSE. World 1 is the safe home — cherry blossom Japan in the World Tree's pink light, no zombies, no PvP, no combat, no danger of any kind, forever. The apocalypse does not leak in, knock, or wait at the fence: it simply does not exist inside the sanctuary. And the moment a keeper steps through the gates beyond World 1, it begins — all of it, at once: the sky goes grey-green, the blossom stops, the ground is cracked, the villages are ruins, and the dead keepers of the old watch shamble between the broken torii in hordes. These are the game's ZOMBIES: the Hollow — fallen guardians the Thorn Sleep wore down past husk, past skeleton, into shambling hunger for the Tree's light (Chapter 1) — joined by their Hollow skeleton kin. They were guardians first; the apocalypse is what the Sleep made of them, and the defense — freeing what can be freed, holding what must be held — is the whole reason the sanctuary has gates at all. One geography, two worlds, and a gate between them: that is the structure every other system in this package hangs on.

Concept art — the transition, in one frame: left, World 1 — the Pink Crystal World Tree, sakura, lanterns lit, stone plaza clean and warm. Center, the great stone gate. Right, beyond it — the apocalypse: cracked earth, dead thorn trees, toppled torii, ruined houses, ash in a grey-green sky, and the horde — zombie figures and Hollow skeletons — shambling in the fog. Pink petals blow through the gate and die in the grey. Build the real transition toward this picture: a player standing in the gateway should be able to see both worlds without moving.
The gates — the only way the worlds touch

The visual shift — paradise to apocalypse, in one walk
The transition is walked, not loaded: no cutscene, no fade to black, no loading screen between a keeper and the end of the world. The last 30 studs inside the gate are a designed gradient — build it as a ramp of small betrayals, so the body understands before the mind does:

The danger ramp — the apocalypse deepens, it never ambushes
Outside is survival combat, but it ramps on rails a new crosser can read: danger is a function of distance from the gate light, announced by the landscape itself. Nobody's first crossing is their last — the apron teaches, the ruins test, the deep ruins are a deliberate expedition, and the Tree-defense raids (Script 31) stage at the outer shrines between the ruins and home, where the horde gathers to walk on the Tree.

Tone, kept even here: the apocalypse is spooky, never gory. Zombies shamble, groan softly, and burst into grey petals and released light when freed — every zombie in this game was a guardian, and freeing one at range is the sniper's whole job (Chapter 36). Players who are overwhelmed are bumped, slowed, and finally folded gently back to the gate apron by the horde's pressure — respawn at the light, counts intact, Daemon at their side. Death is not a word this game uses on its keepers.
Preparing in the safe zone — the expedition loop
Because home is perfectly safe, preparation is a pleasure, not a chore — and the game makes it the heartbeat of every expedition. The plaza notices a party preparing the way a village notices travelers: this is social content, staged in the open, at the Tree.

Quest list for launch

4  The Twin Spear, powers, husks, and Daemon pets
The Twin Spear Pack — twin weapons for twin guardians
Every player receives a spear on spawn, modelled on the twins' own. The design is a true thrusting spear, and every part of it is straight: a LONG dark wood shaft you grip with both hands, one pointed CRYSTAL tip (jade crystal on hers, violet crystal on his, the creator palette colour on a player's), GOLD accent bands and studs spaced along the shaft, and a small gold collar where shaft meets tip. There is no blade and no curve — the weapon only ever goes forward. One tap or click thrusts it. It does not damage players outside the Arena, ever. Against a Thorn Husk it deals 25 — two thrusts free a standard husk — and throws sparkles so a hit is obvious without a health bar lecture. Skins change the tip, trail, and sparkle colour, never damage. Kids stay equal; style is the ladder.
The lore, in-world: the Twin Spears were forged as a PAIR — one great branch of the Great Blossom Tree, split lengthwise, half given to each twin on the day they became guardians — so the Pack is literal: two weapons, one origin, twin guardians. Neither spear is whole alone, and the Grove's oldest carving says it plainly: 'What one tip begins, the other finishes.'

The Twin Spear Pack: two long wood shafts, gold bands and collars, and crystal tips — jade on hers (right), violet on his (left) — held level for the thrust, never swung. Every spear a player carries is built to this picture (Chapter 7, Step 4).

Animation direction (Studio, Animation Editor): carry the spear level, tip forward, resting along the forearm between thrusts — never swung, never sheathed like a sword. Stage 1, Quick Thrust — a fast straight jab: shaft slides through the front hand, tip flashing out and back. Stage 2, Piercing Lunge — the whole body steps in behind the thrust, one committed lunge, tip leading, petals streaming off the shaft. Stage 3, Bloom Thrust — a full lunge that lands with a twist of the shaft, and the petal ring bursts outward as the tip pulls free. Keep all three under the server cooldowns in Script 2 (0.55 s idle, 0.38 s in a chain); the animation sells speed the numbers already allow.

Thorn Husks — the sleepy opposition
Husks are spirits asleep inside thorn-and-wood shells. They wander slowly, never chase far, and deal no damage on touch in the Grove version; in the Arena they bump players back gently. When freed, the shell bursts into petals, a small spirit fox pops out and waves, and the player who landed the freeing thrust earns 25 Shards and 1 Bloom. The code in Chapter 8 implements exactly this behavior, including the 20-second respawn.
Daemon pets — your other self
Every keeper's partner has two scales of one being. At hand scale, it is the COMPANION of Chapter 34: the branch-grown creature paired 1:1 with the keeper's chosen weapon — the wooden sprite, fox, serpent, or bear cub, pink and brown — who walks beside them and transforms into their weapon. At guardian scale, the same being is the DAEMON PET of this chapter: their own Susanoo, condensed into a rideable, flyable crystal bear. It is not a follower, not a summon, and not a second creature — it is the keeper's guardian folded small enough to stand beside them and strong enough to carry them (the full system is Chapter 32), and the companion is that same guardian at the scale of a friend. For every other keeper the Daemon pet lineup is four crystal bear colours — purple, green, pink, and blue — with gold claws, gold trim, and a gold nose and tail tip; the purple skeleton bear with gold teeth is one of those standard variants, a purchasable skeleton-bear design in the Design Package family (Chapter 6), available to any keeper — it is NOT Oakley's pet, and it never was her exclusive. Every keeper's first Daemon is the green crystal bear; the blue is earned in play; the pink is the Daemon Design Package of Chapter 6. Oakley's Daemon is not a bear at all, and she is in no lineup and no rotation: she is a GOLD JAPANESE DRAGON — female, a golden serpentine dragon of polished gold scales, elegant antler horns, long whiskers, and a flowing gold mane — the partner of the protagonist, granted by Oakley's UserId alone and locked exactly like her Green Jade Skeleton (Chapters 9 and 32 name all three of her exclusives). Her brother's Daemon is the blue crystal bear. The Daemon herself is never sold — she is earned, grown, and bonded. Money touches the edges only: the Design Package's pink variant, an Extra Daemon Pet Slot pass (a second Daemon echo out alongside yours, cosmetic only), and Daemon Treats, all in Chapter 6. And Oakley has no branch and no branch companion from Chapter 34's system at all: her partner's resting form is the dragon herself, worn as a scarf on her definitive avatar (Chapter 36), and her weapon form is the Golden Dragon Rifle of Chapter 36 — a maxed-out semi-automatic sniper rifle, the standard weapon-companion law at legendary tier.


The core loadout — weapon and Daemon, one being
Strip the game to its foundation and every player holds the same kit: a WEAPON and a PARTNER. The weapon is their chosen starter (Chapter 34) — spear, katana, scythe, or hammer, designed in the Spirit Workbench. The partner is one being at two scales: the COMPANION creature who transforms into that weapon, and the DAEMON — rideable, flyable, their condensed Susanoo. And the deepest truth of the design, the one every system in this package is built on: the weapon and the partner are the same being. The companion transforms into the weapon in your hands; stow it and it pours back out and stands beside you. Condense the Susanoo and the Daemon stands there instead. One entity, five states, and every change passes through the branch (Chapter 34):

The states are exclusive. The Daemon-scale cycle is one button (G, or the Daemon panel): Beast folds to Weapon; Weapon raises the Susanoo; the Susanoo condenses back to Beast — every Daemon form change takes 2.2 seconds, requires a dismount, and routes through the branch hub (Chapter 34), while the companion-scale fold — companion into weapon and back — rides the equip itself at 0.8 seconds (Script 45). Nothing about any cycle touches the counts, because the counts were never the weapon's or the partner's to hold — they are the player's, as the next section states.
The objective, in one sentence — the sentence the tutorial teaches first and every system repeats: you and your pet defend the Pink Crystal World Tree from the skeletons. The Tree — the Great Blossom Tree, pink crystal, the living heart of the Grove — is what the Hollow skeletons walk for, and its meter (1,000, Script 31) is the mission; the village and statue meters are the wider stakes of the same watch. A raid is WON when the wave is cleared or the 240-second assault runs out with the Tree still standing — a defense held, worth Guardian Essence (Chapter 30). It is LOST at the Tree: if the Tree's meter empties, the Tree Falls, and Script 31 marks it Fallen for every player in the server to see. Everything else in this game — the counts, the zones, the stages, the Stride — exists to make a keeper stronger at exactly this one job.
Two counts, pinned to the player
The game keeps TWO counts per player, stored as two completely independent values, both keyed to the player's UserId — never to a weapon, a character, a Daemon, or an appearance. Switching spears, switching Daemons, changing your whole look at the Workbench: the counts follow the player, permanently, because they were only ever the player's.

One counted thrust credits BOTH counts by one. Spending touches only the Spend Balance. The example to test in Studio: a player at 1,000 Lifetime and 1,000 Spend Balance buys a 300-thrust item. Afterwards: Spend Balance 700, Lifetime still 1,000 — every zone, rank, and Susanoo stage the 1,000 had unlocked stays unlocked. If a build ever shows the Lifetime count moving down, that build is broken, whatever else it does well.
Every number, measured

6  Monetization — what is sold, what is never sold
Two lists run this whole chapter, and they never mix. The sell list: cosmetic skin packs, trails, auras, pets and pet items, and a lounge — bought with Robux through Roblox's own prompts, granted by one server Script (Script 10), and shown in one shop panel (Script 11). The never-sell list has exactly one item on it, and it is named first so there is no ambiguity anywhere later in this package.

The two ways Roblox lets a game sell things

The distinction matters in code, not just in the shop. A pass is a fact the game looks up (UserOwnsGamePassAsync). A product is an event the game must handle exactly once per payment (ProcessReceipt, in Script 10) — grant the item, and only then tell Roblox the receipt is done. Script 10 is the only Script in this game allowed to set ProcessReceipt; Roblox permits exactly one handler, and a second one silently replaces the first.

Compare two or three similar kids' games in the Creator Hub at the moment you create each item, set the price there, and change one price at a time afterwards. Prices are set in the Dashboard, never in code; the code holds only the numeric IDs.
Set it up — Dashboard first, then two ID tables

Do the same under Developer Products for the two consumables. Note every numeric ID the Dashboard assigns — pass IDs and product IDs are different number series; do not mix them.

Then copy each ID into BOTH scripts: the GAME_PASSES / PRODUCTS tables at the top of Script 10 and the ITEMS list in Script 11. The server table decides who owns what; the client list only decides which buy buttons appear.
Any ID left at 0 stays disabled on purpose: Script 11 labels it 'Coming soon' and cannot prompt a purchase, and Script 10 never grants it. A half-configured shop fails safe, exactly like the spirit lock.

Solvency audit — the prices, checked against the faucets and the fees
A game is solvent when three things hold at once: nothing can be minted for free faster than it can be spent, nothing sold is undercut by what play gives away, and the platform's cuts are counted before anyone calls a Robux 'earnings'. This audit checks all three against numbers taken from this package's own code and from Roblox's published terms — re-verify the fee and DevEx figures in the Creator Hub when you set prices, because Roblox changes them on its own schedule, not yours.
The faucets — what free play mints, per hour, at the code's own ceilings

Ceilings are not averages — a real child collects slower, travels between points, and stops for lunch. Ceilings are what an audit must price against, because a ceiling is what a determined player (or a script) can actually reach. Two conclusions fall straight out of the table. First: the 500-Shard Grove Trail is priced in minutes of play, which is correct for an earn-only cosmetic — time is its currency, and it becomes a first-evening goal rather than a grind. Second, and this changed the sell list: Sakura Shards cannot be sold at any sane price. The first edition of this chapter sold 50 Shards for 25 Robux — under a minute of ceiling-rate play, offered to a child for real money. Packs big enough to beat the faucet (thousands of Shards) would instead let one payment flood the earn economy and make every play-earned balance feel worthless. There is no price between those two failures, so the packs were removed. Pet treats and fireworks are sold instead precisely because no faucet mints them: play cannot undercut them, and money cannot buy what play earns.
The fees — what a sale is actually worth
Roblox takes a 30% marketplace fee on in-game pass and product sales: the account is credited 70% of the list price as Earned Robux. Earned Robux are not cash. They convert through DevEx only at or above 30,000 Earned Robux, at the standard rate of $0.0038 per Earned Robux ($114.00 for exactly 30,000) in the terms current when this package was revised — a separate higher rate for qualifying spend by age-checked US adults exists, and this audit deliberately ignores it, because this game's buyers are children and a solvent plan does not count a rate its own audience cannot produce. Roblox may also hold sale Robux as pending before they count as Earned; the Dashboard shows the current state of both rules.

Read the last column as the honesty column. Even a clean sweep of the catalogue at the cheapest pass needs 875 separate buyers before the first DevEx request exists; the game needs 42,858 Robux of gross sales (30,000 ÷ 0.70, rounded up) before one dollar can leave the platform. That is not a reason not to sell — passes also buy goodwill, photos, and return visits — but any plan that treats the first month of sales as income is insolvent on paper before it is insolvent in fact. Until the 30,000 threshold, every Robux earned is platform credit, best spent inside Roblox (advertising the game, for instance) by a decision the parent makes, not by momentum.
Refunds and chargebacks sit outside the game's code: Roblox administers them, and may claw back the Robux. Clean per-purchase records — the receipt ledger in Script 10 — are what a parent shows Roblox support when a sale is disputed.
The rules that do not bend
Cosmetic or convenience only — nothing sold makes a paying player stronger, faster, or better at freeing husks than a playing player. Twin skin passes change colour, never damage.
No loot boxes, no random paid rewards, no gambling-style mechanics — ever. If a reward is random, it is earned in play, never bought.
No limited-time pressure aimed at children: no fake countdowns, no 'your pet is sad' prompts, no purchase pop-ups on respawn, on falling, or on failure. The shop opens only when a player taps Shop.
Every paid item can be previewed for free at the shrine photo stage, so no child has to buy a thing to see what it looks like.
The earn currency is never sold. Shards and Blooms are earned in play only; the moment money can buy the same number play produces, every price in this chapter is being measured against a faucet (see the audit below) — so this game does not sell them at all.
Her exclusive spirit form never appears in the shop panel, the Dashboard, a thumbnail, or the game description as something obtainable. Other players are never teased with a locked item they cannot have.
Earnings note, plainly: Robux earned in a game are converted through Roblox's Developer Exchange, which has its own eligibility rules, minimums, and identity checks for the account holder. The account holder — the parent — handles payouts, taxes, and the account. Verify the current DevEx terms in Creator Hub before counting on any amount, and remember a pass sale and cash in hand are separated by those rules, not by anything in this package.

9  The Headless Jade Spirit — hers only, locked by UserId
This is the trick the catalog will not sell anyone — a truly headless avatar — built legally inside your own game, and in this game it belongs to exactly one person: his daughter. Her real body turns invisible, nothing is added in its place (that empty head slot is the whole secret of headless), and a headless skeleton of clean, polished green jade crystal walks where she walks — blocky jade-crystal ribs, spine, pelvis, arms and legs, faceted green jade crystals set into the crystal blocks, every surface clean and polished — with her pink bow floating above the empty neck so everyone who knows her recognises her instantly. There is no moss on it, no plants, and no organic growth of any kind: not on the shoulders, ribs, pelvis, legs, or feet. Clean jade crystal is the whole finish.
Why the form is the heart of the game, and not a costume: in the Grove's oldest story, the first guardian of the Great Blossom Tree was a keeper who loved the Tree more than her own shape. When the Thorn Sleep came — the long dusk that turns guardians into husks and skeletons — the seal that could hold it back demanded a crown freely given: her head, the seat of her name and face, laid into the Tree's roots. She gave it. The Tree bloomed crystal the same hour, and she has walked the Grove ever since as light in the shape she kept — headless, because the head was the price, and jade, because the Tree remembers her in its own colour. The weeping statue in the plaza is her as the village remembers her before the gift; the Hall of Guardians keeps her empty place at its head. Every player who defends the Tree is, in the story's terms, standing the watch she can no longer stand alone.
Why only she can embody it: the form is not earned, unlocked, or granted — it ANSWERS one person. In the fiction, the guardian's light recognises the keeper it was promised to; in the build, Script 8 recognises exactly one UserId, server-side, fail-closed, the same pattern that guards the twins' signature Daemons. No other player can wear the myth, because the myth is a person. Everyone else aspires to it — that aspiration is the game's emotional engine — and aspiration is served by everything else in this package: the Daemon pets, the Susanoo stages, the zones, the defense. The legend herself stays singular.

The design principle — one rare item, one player
Before the build, the principle that governs it, in full. In Oakley’s look there is ONE rare item: the Headless Jade Skeleton form itself. Not her robes, however beautiful; not her spear, however storied; not her mask, her sash, or her shoulder guards. Those are the frame — designed, deliberate, and lovely — and a frame’s glory is what it shows, never itself. The rarity, the legend, and the thing no one else has is the skeleton: the headless jade form, worn by one player, Oakley, granted by her UserId and by nothing else. The skeleton is the centerpiece; everything else in this package — outfit, Daemon, Tree, village — is arranged around it. Any text, shop, thumbnail, or update that spreads the word rare across the frame has misunderstood the design and must be corrected back to this paragraph.
Its name, as the Grove tells it: the GREEN JADE SKELETON — the heirloom skin, the myth made playable. It is an exclusive skin in the strictest sense this package allows: it belongs to his daughter alone, locked to her UserId by Script 8's server-side check, with no Game Pass, no Developer Product, no price, and no unlock path anywhere in this game (Chapter 6 states the rule as a warning, not a policy). Every player can SEE it — when she walks the plaza in the form, the whole server sees the legend standing among them, and that visibility is the point: the skin is the Grove's founding myth with a player inside it. Nobody else can wear it, earn it, buy it, or borrow it. It is visible to all, wearable by one, and it is never, ever for sale. How the lock works — three layers, server last
Layer 1 — her screen only. Script 9 (the client) checks her UserId before it draws anything. On every other player's device it returns immediately: no button, no B-key or Y-button binding, nothing on screen that hints the form exists in their controls.
Layer 2 — one locked door. Every way of asking for the form — her on-screen button, her B key, her Xbox Y button, the shrine pad, and a cheater firing the RemoteEvent directly from a script — arrives at the same single server function, toggle() in Script 8.
Layer 3 — the server decides. toggle() checks isExclusiveOwner(player) before it touches the character: the player's UserId must equal the one number stored on the server. A client can be modified; a server Script in your game cannot be edited by a player. For anyone else the function simply returns — no error, no message, no partial morph, and nothing that a purchase, a quest, or a code typed in chat can change, because no other system in the game is given the power to grant it. Script 10 (monetization) deliberately contains no reference to the skeleton at all. Accepted toggles are rate-limited to one per second, and the rig template never leaves ServerStorage, which clients cannot see — Chapter 14 walks every spoofing attempt against this lock, one by one.
How the morph works — hide, then weld
Hide, do not delete. Script 8 sets Transparency to 1 on every visible body Part — the Head included — plus the face decal and accessory handles. The Parts and the Motor6D joints of the 15-part R15 body stay exactly where they were, so animations still play, the spear still equips, and the neck joint still moves — it just moves an invisible head.
Weld the jade bones on. A rig you build once in Studio (SpiritRig in ServerStorage) is cloned onto her. Each jade bone is placed on the matching invisible body Part and joined with a WeldConstraint, so the game's own animation moves the bone for free. Crucially, the rig contains no Skull bone, and Script 8 deletes one if it ever finds it in the template — headless is enforced in code, not just in your build discipline. The one visible thing at head height is the pink Spirit Bow, welded to the invisible Head Part so it hovers and bobs where her head would be.

Step 1 — Set her UserId, before anything else. Log in as your daughter on roblox.com, open her profile, and read the number in the address: roblox.com/users/<NUMBER>/profile. Paste that number in place of the 0 on the EXCLUSIVE_USER_ID line near the top of Script 8, and again in the same place in Script 9 (Chapter text below). Write it down nowhere else in the game — not on a sign, not in the description. Until this step is done, leave both numbers at 0: locked for everyone is the safe state.
Step 2 — Make the container. In ServerStorage, insert a Model and name it exactly SpiritRig. Everything in this section goes inside it. Build it on the ground in front of the shrine at player size — the finished spirit form stands about 5 studs tall.
Step 3 — Build one long form part, then the frame. Long form part: a thin cylinder (about 0.28 × 1.0 × 0.28) with a small sphere (0.42 across) at each end; Union the three pieces and name the Union LeftUpperArm; duplicate and rescale for every limb row in the form-part list. Frame: one vertical spine bar of light, one sternum bar at the front, and 5 curved glow arcs — each a flattened Torus mesh, or three thin boxes angled as left curve, front, and right curve — spaced evenly, biggest in the middle; Union all of it as ArcFrame. Pelvis: one wide box. Build every part CLEAN: polished jade crystal only — add NO moss, plant, vine, foliage, or greenery part to any bone, and delete any such part if an early draft has one. Build NO head — and if an early draft of the rig has one, delete it; Script 8 will delete it at runtime anyway, but a clean template keeps the build honest. Add the SpiritBow: two pink wedges and a knot on an invisible-height stand at head position in the template — its exact height is set by Script 8, so approximate placement is fine.
Step 4 — Fit the rig to a body. Insert an R15 Rig from the Avatar tab next to SpiritRig. Drag each form part on top of the body part it welds to — frame arcs over upper torso, pelvis over lower torso, limb parts centred on each limb — sitting just inside the body's outline. The WeldConstraint in Script 8 locks in whatever offset exists when it first runs, so a part placed 0.1 studs off stays 0.1 studs off — the extra minute here is spent once.
Step 5 — Place the shrine pad. In Workspace, add a flat jade Part at the shrine steps named exactly SpiritStation, Anchored ON. Script 8 adds its 'Become the Jade Spirit' prompt automatically. Understand what the pad is: a family keepsake in the world, not a public station — its handler is the locked toggle(), so for every player except her, using it does precisely nothing.
Step 6 — Paste the two scripts and test the lock, not just the look. Script 8 goes in ServerScriptService (rename it HeadlessSpirit); Script 9 is a LocalScript in StarterPlayer → StarterPlayerScripts (rename it HeadlessSpiritToggle). Then test three accounts, in this order: (a) HER account — the button appears bottom-right labelled 'Jade Spirit', B / Y toggles the form, the body is fully invisible, NO head is visible, the pink bow floats and bobs, the jade frame arcs move as she runs and breathes, the spear still thrusts, and toggling off restores her avatar exactly. (b) A SECOND account (yours, or a friend's) — there must be no button at all, B and Y must do nothing, and the shrine pad must do nothing. (c) HER account on Xbox — Y toggles, the A-button shrine prompt appears, and a phone player watching sees the change at the same moment. Do not publish until (b) passes: other players getting nothing is a launch requirement, not a nice-to-have.

Turning it on — three ways, one locked switch

All three fire the same RemoteEvent (JadeSpiritToggle), and only Script 8's locked toggle() ever changes a body — so the button, the controller, and the shrine can never disagree, and none of them can be used to bypass the UserId check. Her state lives on the character as the IsJadeSpirit attribute; respawning resets it to normal, so she chooses the form fresh each life.
How it works on Xbox — no separate version
There is nothing Xbox-specific to build. The game runs on Roblox's servers and replicates the character to every device; Script 8 runs on the server, so when it hides her body and welds the jade form parts on, an Xbox, a phone, and a PC in the same server all see the identical headless spirit form at the identical moment. Publish once from Studio and it is already on Xbox — for her account, and her account alone.
Controls: an Xbox controller is a gamepad to Roblox. Script 9 reads it through UserInputService, which reports the Y button as KeyCode.ButtonY in the same event as a keyboard key — one small block covers PC and Xbox, and Roblox itself draws the shrine's A-button prompt on Xbox, E on PC, and a tap button on touch screens.
Performance: 14 bones plus the bow — every Part CanCollide off and Massless on — add no physics cost and run comfortably on Xbox Series X|S and the oldest supported phones.
The expectation to set once, kindly: the form lives inside this game only. It is not a catalog item, cannot be taken into other people's games, and cannot be given or sold to a friend inside this one either — their accounts are simply not the number in the lock. Inside Jade Spirit it is hers; that is the gift.
If she ever changes accounts, the form does not follow the username — it follows the number. Update EXCLUSIVE_USER_ID in Scripts 8 and 9 to the new account's UserId, republish, and the lock moves with her.
Script 8 — HeadlessSpirit: the UserId lock and the headless morph (server)
Location: ServerScriptService → insert Script, rename it HeadlessSpirit. Set EXCLUSIVE_USER_ID at the top before testing — while it is 0, nobody can morph, including you.

Script 9 — HeadlessSpiritToggle: her button, B key, and Xbox Y button (client)

Troubleshooting — lock problems first, looks second
She has no button: the two EXCLUSIVE_USER_ID numbers disagree, or both are still 0. Script 9's number controls her screen; Script 8's controls the morph. Set both to the number from her profile address — the digits, not her username.
She has a button but tapping does nothing: Script 8's number is wrong (the server is refusing, exactly as designed). Check Script 8 first — its check is the one that matters — then confirm you tested with her account, not yours.
Another player CAN morph: stop — unpublish (set the place Private) and check two things. One: Script 8 in the live game is this exclusive version, not the old public draft (the header of the exclusive version says EXCLUSIVE VERSION). Two: her ID was not pasted into a copy of the script that grants by username or by group rank in some other Script. There is no fix in the shop or Dashboard for this; the lock is code, and the code is where you check.
A head appears on her spirit form: a Head part survived in the SpiritRig template from an early build. Script 8 deletes one at runtime, so a visible head means the live Script 8 is an older version — repaste this chapter's Script 8 and delete the Head from the template for cleanliness.
Moss, plants, or greenery appear on her skeleton: a growth part survived in the SpiritRig template from an early draft. The canonical avatar is clean polished jade crystal, with no organic growth at all — delete every moss, plant, vine, and foliage part from SpiritRig and rebuild the affected part clean. Do not recolour growth jade and leave it on.
Bones left standing at spawn: a bone was Anchored, or its name differs from the bone list. Unanchor it and check the name first, in that order.
Bow missing or sitting at her feet: the SpiritBow part is missing from SpiritRig, or it was parented under a bone that was deleted with the skull. It must sit directly in the SpiritRig Model; Script 8 positions and welds it to the Head Part itself.
Bones lag one step behind the body: a hand-made Weld survived in the rig alongside Script 8's WeldConstraints. Delete every weld inside SpiritRig — the script must be the only thing joining bones to the body.

14  Security — hardened by design, audited script by script
This game will be public, it takes real money, and it contains one item that must belong to one child forever. Those three facts define the security work. This chapter is the audit: the rules every Script follows, what was found and fixed in each one, how the exclusive lock resists spoofing, and the exploit tests to run before publishing. Every script in this package — all fifty — already contains the hardening described here; the tables below audit them in order, and this chapter is the map that explains why they look the way they do.
The five rules nothing in this game may break
The server decides; the client asks. Every value that matters — currency, quest progress, checkpoint stage, pass ownership, the spirit lock — is computed and stored by server Scripts. Clients render, prompt, and request. A player running a modified client can change what their own screen shows and nothing else.
No client input ever names an amount, an item, or a price. The game's RemoteEvents carry requests and catalogue IDs at most — a toggle, a style ID, a slot number — and every handler re-derives the amount, the price, and the entitlement from server constants before anything moves. Every grant amount in the game is a constant typed into a server Script. An exploiter cannot 'fire an event with a bigger number' because no trusted number ever travels in an event.
Every handler re-derives who is asking. Server code takes the player from the engine — GetPlayerFromCharacter on a real character, the connection-supplied argument of OnServerEvent, GetPlayerByUserId inside ProcessReceipt — and re-checks aliveness, distance, ownership, and state at the moment of the grant, not from anything cached by the client.
Prompts are not proof. ProximityPrompts can be fired from across the map by modified clients, so each prompt handler (Scripts 6, 7, and the shrine in Script 8) verifies on the server that the character is genuinely within reach before anything moves. Tool.Activated is client-initiated, so Script 2 re-derives the wielder and applies the rate limit on the server.
Fail closed, and say so. An unloaded DataStore session cannot save and cannot receive paid grants; an ID left at 0 disables the item and the exclusive form alike; a receipt that cannot be recorded is answered NotProcessedYet rather than granted on trust. Everywhere this package had to choose between 'works during an outage' and 'cannot be exploited during an outage', it chose the second, and the code comments say why at the exact line where the choice is made.
Every script, audited




Why the exclusive lock cannot be spoofed
Walk the attacks, because 'trust the server' is a slogan until it is tested against each one:
Copy her name. Usernames and display names are duplicable — players style them to look identical. The lock never reads a name. It compares player.UserId, the permanent account number Roblox's backend assigns at join, which no client supplies and no profile edit changes.
Fire the RemoteEvent directly. Exploit tools can fire JadeSpiritToggle without the button. OnServerEvent hands the server the Player object for the connection that fired it — the attacker's own — and toggle() checks that object's UserId first. Extra arguments are ignored by the handler's signature, so firing FireServer(herPlayer) is decoration: the event still arrives wearing the attacker's identity.
Set the attribute. Clients can set attributes on instances they own and can fake any local state. Nothing on the server ever grants from HasHeadlessJadeSpirit or IsJadeSpirit — those are outputs the server writes. toggle() recomputes from UserId on every single call, so there is no cached 'unlocked' state to flip.
Copy the game files. Every client receives the game's client scripts and replicated assets; assume they are public (they are). The rig template is therefore kept in ServerStorage, which is never replicated, and Script 8 itself lives server-side where its contents and the pasted UserId are not sent to clients. What a copied file could contain — the mechanism — is worthless to an attacker without a place of their own to run it in, and in their own place the ID they would have to paste is still hers alone to benefit from in this game: the lock travels with the number, not the file.
Spam the toggle. Rig cloning is the one expensive thing the system does, so accepted toggles are limited to one per second per player and re-verify a living character. Spam from anyone else costs one failed comparison per event.
Social-engineer the setup. The one genuine vulnerability is human: the ID must be pasted into Scripts 8 and 9 by the parent, and a screenshot of Script 8's top lines would show it. Treat that number like an account detail — knowing it grants an outsider nothing (they cannot become that UserId), but there is no reason to publish it, and the game description, signs, and thumbnails must never carry it.
Receipt discipline — exactly once, or not yet
ProcessReceipt is the one function where a bug is denominated in money, so its six steps are printed in its header and summarised here: in-session set first (a repeat in the same session is answered Granted with no second grant); a persistent DataStore ledger keyed by PurchaseId, read before granting — a read failure answers NotProcessedYet, never a blind grant; a ledger hit means an earlier session already granted; the product must be in the allowlist or routed to a grant function that owns its ID, purchased in this place, for a player whose data has loaded; the grant is a table constant; and the PurchaseId is recorded BEFORE PurchaseGranted is returned, with a failed record write again answering NotProcessedYet so Roblox redelivers into the ledger's protection. The residual window — grant completed, record lost to a simultaneous store failure, redelivery arriving in a later session to an empty ledger — is the known limit of check-then-record ordering; it is narrow, it favours the paying player rather than the house, and if it is ever observed the ledger plus Roblox's own transaction history give the parent what is needed to reconcile by hand.
Anti-duplication sweep — the whole economy, one list

Before you publish — the exploit test protocol
Run these with a second account (never hers) in the private build. Each test names its pass condition; a single failure means fix, retest, and only then publish.
Skeleton lock: on the second account — no button on screen; press B and (with a controller) Y: nothing. Walk to the shrine pad and use the prompt: nothing. This account must finish the session never having seen the form in its own controls.
Prompt distance: with any executor-free method available to you (a second device walking away mid-test is enough for the honest version), confirm the shop and quest prompts do nothing once the character is beyond reach — the server checks in Scripts 6 and 7 are what you are exercising; then repeat standing at the pad and confirm they work.
Double-fire: tap the shop prompt and the quest prompt rapidly and repeatedly. One charge, one grant, one quest reward — watch Shards before and after and do the arithmetic out loud.
Rejoin persistence: buy the cheapest product in the private build, note the bag counts, leave, rejoin. Counts unchanged, pass effects present, and no second delivery of the product.
Receipt honesty (Studio): in Studio's test purchase flow, complete a product purchase, then stop and restart the test session and complete the flow again for the same test receipt if the tools offer it — the ledger must prevent a double grant. At minimum, confirm in the Output window that ProcessReceipt runs once per purchase and answers are logged without errors.
Data-outage behaviour: this one is a code re-read, not a live test — confirm Script 1's DataSaveDisabled path and Script 10's DataLoaded gate are present in the copies you pasted. The failure they prevent (a zeroed balance saved over a real one) only happens during a real outage, which is exactly when you cannot improvise.
The numbers on the wall: before setting the place Public, re-read Chapter 6's fee table against the Dashboard's current marketplace fee and DevEx terms. If Roblox has changed either number since this package was revised, update the Dashboard prices with the new arithmetic first — the audit's method survives rate changes; its figures may not.

28  The Spirit Workbench — character creation, Heavy Is The Crown style
The workbench philosophy, carried over from Heavy Is The Crown: a character is not picked from a menu, it is built on a bench — chassis first, material second, then a slider that walks the piece from blueprint wireframe to finished bloom, and a lighting check before anything is confirmed. The philosophy is what transfers; no code, assets, or models from that project are used here. Everything in this chapter is built fresh for the Grove, in the Grove's own parts and palette.
The creator lives at a physical workbench in the village, near the shops — a place players walk to, the way the statue is a place and the Tree is a place. A Create button opens the same window for players who find it first. Either way, the window (Script 34) is a catalogue and a preview; the building happens on the server (Script 33) or not at all — Chapter 29 is the lock on that door.
The six chassis — silhouette is the choice

Scales are session character scales set by the server from this table — the player's account avatar is never edited, and Remove restores the exact default scale set. There is no seventh chassis. In particular there is no spirit-form chassis, no headless option, and no way to remove the head: every preview mannequin and every applied look includes a head, because the one headless form in this game is not a style.
The ten materials — finish, not anatomy

A naming note, chosen deliberately: the pale material is Bone Porcelain — a smooth ceramic finish, like a teacup. It is a surface on a normal, complete avatar. It is not bone anatomy, it builds no ribs and no skull, and it cannot be combined with anything in this system to approximate her form, because the system contains no anatomical parts at all — it builds a sash, two shoulder guards, a torso plate, and a light ring.
The detail slider — blueprint to full bloom
One slider, five stops — the stops are the design, because each is a build stage the player can feel under their thumb:

Colour — a twelve-colour palette, three slots
Twin, Aura, and Effects each take one colour from the same twelve-name palette Script 33 carries: PetalPink, BlossomHot, JadeGlow, PaleJade, BlossomGold, SoftGold, SkyCrystal, Lavender, KoiOrange, LeafGreen, PearlWhite, Charcoal. Players pick swatches; the client sends the palette NAME, never an RGB value — there is deliberately no free colour picker, because a free picker is a value the server would have to trust or range-check, and a name on a list needs neither. The palette is generous enough to feel personal and small enough to stay inside the game's art direction: no combination of twelve curated colours can clash with the Grove.
Lighting preview — day, night, grove
Three preview lights, matching the game's own rhythm: Day (bright sky), Night (the deep blue the corruption prefers), and Grove (warm lantern green-gold). The preview changes only the window's ViewportFrame lighting — it never touches Lighting service state, the player's camera, or any client setting (this chapter's rule: a preview is a place, not a preference). A look is confirmed only after the player has seen it under the light they care about; the turntable buttons rotate the mannequin 30° per tap.
The Mask Atelier — masks are customizable
Below the chassis and materials sits the Mask Atelier strip. Every player designs their own mask from five choices, all of them catalogue IDs: base shape, material, palette colour, glow, and motif. The mannequin wears each choice the instant it is tapped, under all three preview lights.

The five base shapes, one per material: Angular in jade, Curved in pink crystal, Beast in bone, Helm in iron with gold trim, and the wooden Half-Mask. Colour, glow, and motif are layered on top by the player — the shape is the silhouette, the rest is personality.

Mask part construction in Studio
Script 33 builds player masks from part recipes on the server, so there is nothing to model for the system itself — but build one DISPLAY set on the workbench mannequin so players can walk around real masks before designing. Build each shape on a spare R15 head at the bench, using these parts (all unanchored, CanCollide off — they are display copies):
Angular: Plate box (1.50 × 1.05 × 0.16) on the face, Brow band across the top, a WedgePart nose guard, two stepped Cheek boxes, and a Chin box. The stepped edges are the style — keep the steps visible.
Curved: a wider Plate (1.55 × 1.10), a rounded TopRoll band, and two Side panels hugging the cheeks; smaller wedge nose. Everything sits closer to the face than Angular.
Beast: Plate riding higher, a heavy Brow, two WedgePart ears at the top corners, a Snout box low on the face, and a Jaw band under it. The Fang motif bolts straight onto this jaw.
Helm: Plate plus a Crown band floating a stud above it, and two long Guard panels running down past the jaw — the knightly silhouette. The crown band takes the accent colour.

Weapon & wing design — the guardian sections
The last two strips of the workbench design the player's GUARDIAN, not their avatar. Weapon: the TYPE is not designed here — it is chosen first, at the Threshold (Chapter 34): spear, katana, scythe, or hammer. The Daemon Atelier — designing your other self
The Workbench's final strip designs the Daemon pet itself, as fully as any figure in the game: colour (the four lineup crystals and the palette beyond them), material (the crystal finishes), scale, glow, claws (the gold accent sets), accessory, and FORM — the solid crystal beast, in every variant a keeper may own. 29  Creator security — a whitelist, or nothing
The creator is the most inviting attack surface in the game — a system whose whole job is letting players change how they look — so it is built backwards from the usual design: instead of accepting a configuration and checking it for bad parts, it accepts nothing that is not already on a list. Creative freedom inside the walls; outside the walls there is no door, only a wall.
The payload — twenty-six fields, all of them IDs

Notice what the schema does not contain: no asset ID, no part or mesh name, no Color3, no texture, no scale number, no UserId. A tampered client cannot inject an unauthorized asset because the language it is allowed to speak has no word for one. Sending a field outside the twenty-six fails an exact key-count check; sending an unlisted value fails the catalogue lookup; both are logged with the player's UserId and the specific reason, and three rejections inside a minute lock that player's creator access for sixty seconds. Nothing about a rejection is shown to other players, and nothing is ever granted partially — a configuration is built whole from server constants or not at all.
Validated four times, not once
On apply: validateConfig rebuilds the configuration from catalogue constants — even a passing client table contributes nothing but its choices, because the server's copy is a fresh table, not the client's.
On equip: every TwinSpear equip and every JadeCreator_* part appearing on a character triggers a sweep of that character.
On respawn: the stored profile is re-validated against today's whitelist before it is applied — a profile saved under an older, looser build cannot smuggle yesterday's rules into today's game.
Every 15 seconds: the sweep re-derives the expected look (exact part names per Detail stop, exact colours, exact scale values) from the stored profile and repairs or removes anything that differs. Tampered scales are reset from the catalogue; unapproved JadeCreator_* parts are destroyed and logged.
Two boundaries are stated plainly so nobody over-trusts the system. First, the whitelist governs what the creator builds; the player's own avatar, clothing, and accessories are theirs and are never scanned for removal — the creator's authority begins and ends at instances named JadeCreator_*. Second, a client can always alter what IT alone renders; that is true of every Roblox game and harms no one, because the replicated look — what every other player sees — is server-built and sweep-repaired. What the sweep protects is the shared world, and the shared world is the one that matters.
Exclusive assets are unreachable from here
The spirit rig lives in ServerStorage under Script 8's control; the creator has no reference to it, no shared remote, and no catalogue entry that names it. A payload string like a spirit part name is simply not one of the approved catalogue IDs, so it dies at the same lookup as any typo. Script 33 additionally checks IsJadeSpirit before building and clears its own parts rather than touch her form. And the alignment system of Chapter 30 was kept out of this schema on purpose: there is no Alignment field, so there is nothing for a client to set, spoof, or argue about — his violet guardian is decided by a UserId comparison on a server, exactly like her spirit form.

Script 34 — CharacterCreatorGui: catalogue, slider, preview (client)

The five stages — earned in thrusts and essence

Two currencies of effort, both un-buyable: Lifetime thrusts (which spending never reduces, Chapter 4) gate the early stages; Guardian Essence — +2 per Hollow skeleton laid to rest, +15 per Hollow boss, +5 per defense held — gates the armoured stages, so the perfect form belongs to players who actually fight the corruption, not only to players who thrust at trees. The shield: while manifested, the guardian absorbs damage before the player's health does — 25 points at Stage 1 up to 125 at Stage 5 — regenerating 5 points every 2 seconds. The absorb hook checks the wielder's position first: inside the Blossom Arena it does nothing at all.

Visibility is the social layer: a Stage 5 guardian over the plaza tells every new player exactly what dedication looks like, the way her spirit form does — except this legend, anyone can earn.
Appearance — the Susanoo IS your design, manifested
The Susanoo is not a separate creature with its own look. Script 33 publishes the design as attributes; Script 35 rebuilds the rig the moment it changes. Change your design at the workbench and your giant changes with you: identity, scaled up. Three systems, one design flow.
The twins' guardians — fixed designs, purple jade and all
There are exactly two beings in this game whose guardian does not take its design from the workbench: the twins. Hers is fixed — jade guardian, the classic long wood spear with a JADE crystal tip, and ONE pink crystal wing, exactly her portrait grown giant. The truth at the center of this chapter, stated plainly: a keeper's Daemon pet is not a pet, not a summon, and not a second creature. One being, three states. It was never two things, and it was never only a tool: the Daemon is a partner, with a partner's habits — it looks at its keeper first when it wakes, and it shakes itself once, every time it comes back, the way it has since the first morning of the Grove.
