Where every Susanoo element goes


Three states of one being

The states are exclusive, enforced in one place (Script 39): Beast, Weapon, and Susanoo — exactly one at a time, tracked per player as the DaemonState attribute and readable by any script through _G.JadeDaemonForm. The cycle is one input (G, or the Daemon panel): Beast with the spear in hand folds to Weapon; Weapon raises the Susanoo; the Susanoo condenses back to Beast — and with the spear stowed, Beast unfolds straight to the Susanoo. While condensed in either small form, Script 35's rig and shield are suppressed through _G.JadeSetSusanooForm, and Script 35's own manifest toggle refuses to raise a second body next to the first.
The transformation — animation and rules

Request: the Daemon panel button, G key, or Xbox ButtonX (Script 40). The request carries no arguments; Script 39 re-checks Stage ≥ 2, a living character, and a 6-second cooldown, every time — and decides the palette the way it decides everything about a Daemon: the keeper's own design and unlocks, with the twins' signatures settled server-side by UserId, fail-closed.
EVERY FORM CHANGE REQUIRES THE DISMOUNT. If the keeper is in the RiderSeat — or a passenger is still aboard — the request is refused, silently. The Daemon unfolds around a standing guardian, never around a seated one. Dismount first (prompt, or stand), step clear, then transform.
Condensing works anywhere the keeper stands; the Daemon arrives at their side. Respawning wakes the keeper with the partner folded to its BRANCH beside them (Chapter 34) — the branch is the resting state every return passes through; at Stage 2+ the first transform request blooms straight through Companion to Beast.
Nothing transforms in the Blossom Arena's player-facing sense: expansion there is allowed, but Script 35's own rule already zeroes its bonuses inside the Arena, and Daemon claws never damage players anywhere. The toggle is spectacle and stance, never an Arena exploit.
The partnership — your Daemon is a person
Design Oakley’s Daemon as a character, not a vehicle — and design her as HER: the Gold Dragon is female, and the partnership prose, the panel, and the Studio notes all call her she. (Every keeper’s bear Daemon is likewise a person with the same three habits; only Oakley’s partner is a dragon.) She has habits a player can learn to read: the Answer (she looks at her keeper first, in the first 0.4 seconds of every transformation), the Shake (once, on every return — the same beat whether she unfolds from the Susanoo or pours back out of the spear), and the Wake (her eyes light before any other part when she condenses). In Studio these are three animation beats on the Daemon rig, built once and reused by every transform in Script 39. Players bond with consistency: a Daemon that always greets you the same way stops being a mount inside a week.
The fold into the weapon is a conversation in three beats, inside the same 2.2 seconds as every transform: the CALL — the keeper raises the spear hand, and the Daemon's ears and eyes answer — for the dragon, her head lifts and her whiskers flare; the POUR — the Daemon's elements fold in reverse build order and stream into the weapon's quartz: for a companion creature, its signature part last; for the dragon, her tail pours first, her coils unwind ring by ring into gold light, her scales hang in the pour as the hammer's gold bands, and her head goes last — into the pommel — because the dragon's pride leaves the world last (Chapter 36 has her full forging sequence); and the BLAZE — the quartz takes the Daemon's colour and light (Script 39's paintWeapon, with its PointLight), and for a moment the weapon is visibly more than a weapon. The return reverses it: the light pours out, a bear rebuilds paws-first — the dragon rebuilds head-first, coils settling ring by ring — and the Shake closes the conversation.
Resonance is the bond made mechanical — the Soul Eater sync between wielder and living weapon. Every connecting thrust raises the pair's sync by 8 (the panel shows it as a percentage), because acting together is what sync is; it decays at 6 per second, because a bond cools when it is not used. Sync builds in any form. It is spent in exactly one place: in Weapon form, at 100%, the next thrust against a husk or a Hollow skeleton SURGES — the Daemon strikes through the spear for 50 instead of 25, and the sync falls to 40 (Scripts 2 + 39, _G.JadeDaemonSurge). The honesty rules hold: husks and skeletons only, never players; earned by rhythm, never bought; and available to every keeper on the same terms, because it is not a stat — it is a relationship, practiced.
Flight — earned, never given
Flight is a progression unlock, and the game says so from the first hour: “you can fly eventually.” Every player starts grounded. The unlock path is the Susanoo's own growth — flight is not a separate skill tree, it is what a grown Daemon does:

The flight tutorial is one minute at the Tree. The moment a keeper reaches Stage 3, the Daemon panel teaches instead of telling: ride, press F, climb. The first climb is aimed at the World Tree's canopy — the crown every grounded player has been looking up at since spawn — and the Sky Canopy zone (gated at 1,000 Lifetime, crossed on foot by younger keepers) becomes the flyer's first highway. Falling is never punished: release F and the pair glides down on the same wings, and Script 21's air bursts work in every form, with the fourth reserved for a condensed Daemon.
What flight changes — and what it does not. Exploration opens vertically: canopy pickups, zone shortcuts, the Sanctum's high road. Defense gains an angle: during a Hollow assault a flyer can cross the plaza in seconds and free skeletons at the Tree's crown. But the numbers refuse to move: thrust range is still 10, damage is still 25, and the skeletons stay grounded and keep walking for the meters — flight is a better angle on the one objective, never an escape from it. A flyer who will not land still loses the Tree.
Riding — seats, speed, and maneuverability
RiderSeat is a VehicleSeat set into the saddle hollow on the Daemon's back: throttle drives it forward and back, steering turns it. The Daemon's legs are the engine — speed and turn rate come from the stage table in Script 39, not from the seat — so the Daemon handles exactly as well as the Susanoo has grown, and no better:

Sprint is hold-Shift (or Xbox ButtonB) while driving, sent by Script 40 and honored by the server only from the player actually in the RiderSeat. Stamina drains 32/s sprinting and regenerates 22/s otherwise — about three seconds of sprint per full bar, earned back by riding easy. Turning tightens with stage because a bigger guardian folds into a surer-footed Daemon: at Stage 5 it turns at 3.1 rad/s at full speed, where a Stage 2 Daemon must be steered wide. Behind the rider, PassengerSeat carries any one other player — a friend, a sibling, a new player being shown the Grove at Daemon speed. The passenger rides; only the keeper drives, and only their own Daemon carries them.
The Mount Chain — rider and bear, comboing together
Riding is not a taxi service; it is a fighting stance — and it is the core fantasy with its sleeves rolled up: you and your pet, fighting as one unit. Script 2 reports every connecting thrust to Script 39 (_G.JadeDaemonThrust). If the keeper is mounted — or standing within 12 studs of their Daemon — the Daemon ANSWERS: a quarter-second later, its massive gold front claws swipe the nearest Thorn Husk within 9 studs. Rider thrust, Daemon swipe, rider thrust, Daemon swipe — an alternating chain with its own name, the Mount Chain:
The window: a swipe landing within 1.0 s of the connecting thrust extends the chain by 1. Miss the window — no husk in the Daemon's reach, or the rider stops thrusting — and the chain resets. The Daemon panel (Script 40) shows the chain live, from the server's own count.
The multiplier: every 5th chain link grants +5 bonus thrusts through Script 13's bonus grant — Spend Balance only, once per chain at each multiple of 5. Lifetime, ranks, and titles are never touched, so the chain buys spending power at the Thrust Shop, never standing.
The damage: claw damage is the stage table's (15 / 20 / 28 / 38), husks and skeletons only, stamped with the same creator-tag pattern Script 2 uses — a Daemon-freed husk pays its keeper exactly like a thrust-freed one, and Script 4's paid latch still makes a second payment impossible.
Fairness, unchanged: the Daemon cannot hurt players, cannot be hurt (it is a form, not a target — its health is set dressing), and does nothing in a server without its keeper in it. Passenger aboard or not, the chain belongs to the keeper and their Daemon alone.
How the Daemon grows — it doesn't level; the Susanoo grows
There is no Daemon XP, no Daemon level, and no second progression track to grind, because there is no second creature to progress. The Daemon's speed, turning, claw damage, and size ARE the Susanoo stage table (Chapter 30): lifetime thrusts and Guardian Essence grow the guardian, and the folded forms inherit every step the moment it happens — a Stage Up announcement while condensed means the Daemon under you just got faster, surer, and harder-clawed, and the spear in your hand carries the same growth into Weapon form. This is the design's whole elegance: one progression, three bodies. Feed the giant (thrusts, essence, defense, the Hollow) and the Daemon grows; ride the Daemon (Mount Chains, exploration) and the thrusts you land feed the giant back.

34  The First Choice — choose your weapon, meet your companion
Before anything else — before the tutorial, before the Daemon Garden, before a new keeper sets foot in World 1 — they choose their weapon. That is the corrected order of a keeper's life, and this chapter builds it: the Threshold where the choice happens, the four starter characters it offers, and the law that governs everything after it. ONE BEING, THREE FORMS. Every keeper's partner begins as a BRANCH of the World Tree — dark wood, blossoms of pink quartz — which GROWS into a living COMPANION creature, and the companion transforms, Soul Eater-style, into the WEAPON: a single object of wood and pink quartz in the keeper's hands. The branch, the companion, and the weapon are never three things and never two at once: equip the weapon and there is no companion standing beside you, because your companion is in your hands; stow it and the weapon pours back out through the branch and stands beside you again, itself.

The Threshold — where the game actually begins
The Threshold is a small, quiet place that is not in World 1: a round wooden platform under one great overhanging branch of the World Tree, four wooden stands in an arc, and nothing else — no shops, no quests, no NPCs, no timers. A first-time player spawns here (Script 43 holds them here, kindly and completely) with the selection screen open. Returning players never see it again: a saved choice releases them straight to the Grand Torii, and the Threshold stands empty in their world. Build it once, in Studio: a Folder named Threshold in Workspace, a SpawnLocation named ThresholdSpawn on the platform, four display stands (the weapon models of the next section, built at display scale, anchored, purely decorative), and a second SpawnLocation named ThresholdExitSpawn at the Grand Torii in World 1 — Script 43's release target. The exit is not a door the player walks through; choosing is the door.
The selection screen — one decision, made deliberately
Script 44 draws four large cards, one per starter. Each card shows the weapon's name, the companion it wakes, one line of temperament, three plain feel bars (Reach, Swing, Speed), and the damage line — 25, printed on every card, identical, because that is the truth of this game: the choice is about feel and friendship, never power. Tapping a card previews it — the card enlarges, the confirm button arms with the weapon's name — and only a second, deliberate tap on CONFIRM chooses. There is no default selection, no countdown, no skip button, and nothing to buy on this screen or anywhere near it. On Xbox the D-pad moves between cards and A previews and confirms. The moment the server saves the choice, three things happen in order: the gate opens (the player steps out at the Grand Torii), a branch of the World Tree lowers beside them and floats at their left side, and — 1.6 seconds later, in the Root Plaza, in front of everyone — the branch grows into their companion, who looks at them first. The tutorial (Chapter 3) begins from there, with the companion already at their side.

The count keeps its Grove name — thrusts — whatever weapon lands the hit; the Grove named the count for the twins' spears long before it offered a choice, and the name is a memorial, not a mechanism. The bond is the Soul Eater truth made mechanical: the weapon is a person, and fighting together is a rhythm the pair practices. It runs on the numbers Chapter 32 already keeps — Script 39's Resonance: every connecting hit raises sync by 8; sync decays at 6 per second; at 100, in weapon form, the next hit against a husk or a Hollow skeleton surges for 50 and sync falls to 40. A ghillie suit exists for one reason: to make a sniper disappear into the ground she is guarding. Camouflage mechanics — how the blending works

How the ghillie works with her sniper gameplay
The ghillie and the rifle are one system. The rifle (below) reaches across the whole defense field; the ghillie lets her occupy that field unseen while she uses it. Her loop, played from the ghillie: SETTLE — take a perch or a root line with a sightline to the Tree, go still, let the strips lie flat (2 seconds). WATCH — through the max scope, mark the wave: her scoped view tags Hollow skeletons for her whole server (a small blossom marker over each tagged skeleton, visible to every keeper — the guardian's gift is information). FIRE — semi-auto light bolts (below), each shot lifting her blend, the muzzle shimmer flaring iridescent for a heartbeat. MOVE — between volleys, relocate along the root lines while the Hollow walk to where she was; settle again somewhere the blossom is thick. A keeper on the ground sees a wave thin out from nowhere and blossom markers bloom over the survivors: that is Oakley, working. The ghillie turns the defense game (Script 31) into a guardian's overwatch: she is the reason the Tree's far side is never undefended, and the reason a raid's second wave arrives already marked.
Her weapon — the Golden Dragon Rifle: a maxed-out semi-automatic sniper rifle
Oakley's weapon is not the hammer and not the whip — both are retired, completely, and nothing of them remains in her build. Her dragon transforms, Soul Eater-style, into a MAXED-OUT SEMI-AUTOMATIC SNIPER RIFLE: a legendary-tier long rifle of polished gold, built to Oakley's own reference — a warm copper-gold receiver covered in elegant swirling GOLD FILIGREE engravings, an ornate curved gold stock, a black ribbed grip, a long engraved barrel housing, and a large premium telescopic scope in matching gold. MAXED OUT is a build state, not a mood: every upgrade node on the rifle is filled, every attachment slot is occupied by its best attachment, and nothing about it can be upgraded further — there is no higher version of this weapon, for anyone, at any price. 37  Creativity rewards — originality is a progression path
Jade Spirit rewards two kinds of mastery. The counts (Chapter 4) reward persistence: thrusts landed, zones unlocked, stages earned. This chapter rewards the other kind — CREATIVITY. A keeper who designs a character nobody has seen, builds a plot the plaza detours to visit, frees a husk with a combination nobody taught them, or customizes a companion into something with a point of view is progressing — really progressing, with ranks, titles, and currency to show for it — exactly as surely as the keeper grinding the Arena. Creativity here is not decoration on top of the progression system. It IS a progression system: a second ladder beside the counts, with its own ranks (below), its own currency grants, its own contests, and unlocks that exist nowhere else. The design rule that keeps it honest is the same one that keeps everything else honest: creativity is judged by PEOPLE (community votes, never an algorithm and never a purchase), paid in Spend Balance only (Lifetime never moves except by a landed thrust, Chapter 4), and no creative reward can ever be bought, traded in, or granted by a Game Pass.
The four creative paths

Design contests — the weekly rhythm

Rewards — titles, currency, and unlocks that only creativity grants

Creativity ranks — the second ladder
Contest results accumulate into a standing CREATIVITY RANK, displayed beside the keeper's titles and on their profile next to their counts — the two ladders side by side, so the plaza can read both kinds of mastery at a glance. Rank is computed server-side from contest history (entries, votes received, finalist finishes, wins) and, like Lifetime, it never decreases and can never be bought, traded, or transferred.

Why this chapter exists, in one paragraph for the design wall: a grind ladder alone teaches players that time is the only currency. Jade Spirit's world — a sanctuary built around a tree that grows things — should teach the other lesson too: that what you IMAGINED counts. The creativity ladder costs the game nothing it values (Spend Balance is faucet-fed by play anyway, titles are words, unlocks are capacity) and buys the thing every living game needs and cannot purchase: players making things the developers never thought of, in public, where other players can see them do it. When a new keeper asks what there is to do here, the plaza can now answer twice: get stronger — and get original. Both are progression. Only one of them surprises anybody.

38  Progression gating — the count and the partner, in sync
Two locks guard every advanced weapon in Jade Spirit, and BOTH must open before a keeper's hand closes on it. The first lock is the COUNT: every weapon tier carries a minimum Lifetime thrust count (Chapter 4), and a keeper below it cannot wield that tier — not at 100 thrusts, not on a friend's account, not through any shop. The second lock is the PARTNER: your companion — your pet, your meister — has a PET LEVEL, and the weapon's tier must not exceed it. A Tier 4 weapon in the hands of a keeper whose companion is Pet Level 2 does not fire, swing, or transform: the companion will not pour into a form it cannot yet hold, and the weapon stays asleep. This is the Soul Eater law of Chapter 34 applied to progression: the weapon is a person, a person has a level, and the meister and the weapon must be IN SYNC. Neither lock can be bought open (Chapter 6), traded open, or voted open (Chapter 37) — counts rise by thrusts and pet levels rise by the growth Chapters 30 and 32 already track. What follows is the full gating system: the tiers, both requirement tables, and exactly what happens when the two don't match.
Weapon tiers — five, and what a tier means
A weapon's tier is the tier of its DESIGN: the materials, finishes, quartz work, and manifested presence the Workbench (Chapter 28) can put into it — Classic starters at Tier 1 up to Legendary designs at Tier 5. Tier is not a damage ladder (damage lives in Chapters 4 and 36, under their own rules); tier is a mastery ladder. Higher tiers are heavier with light: more of the Grove's power shaped into one object, which is precisely why both the keeper's record and the partner's growth gate them.

Gate 1 — the count requirement (Lifetime thrusts)

The counts are LIFETIME counts, with everything Chapter 4 promises about them: spending Spend Balance never lowers them, so a gate once passed is passed forever. A keeper cannot pick up a Legendary design at 100 thrusts for the same reason they cannot fly at Stage 1: the number is the record of a guardian who has done the work, and the weapon reads the record, not the wish.
Gate 2 — the pet level requirement (your meister must match)
PET LEVEL is the readable number for your companion's growth: computed server-side from ONE input only — your Lifetime thrust count (the full wiring and mapping table are two sections below; there is no pet experience bar). It displays on the companion panel (Script 46) beside the bond, and it never decreases.


One number drives everything — pet level IS your swing count, read aloud
State the wiring plainly, because it is the simplification the whole system stands on: PET LEVEL IS A DIRECT FUNCTION OF LIFETIME THRUSTS. There is no pet experience bar. There is no separate pet grind, no pet food that levels, no second track to feed after the first. Your companion grows because YOU swung — every counted thrust you have ever landed is already inside your partner's level, automatically, the instant it lands. One number — the same Lifetime count that gates the zones (Script 19), the Susanoo stages (Chapter 30), and the weapon tiers (above) — drives everything, and the pet level is simply that number, translated into the partner's language:

Why one number is better than two tracks — the design argument, once, plainly: two-track progression (your XP plus your pet's XP) always decays into one real track and one chore, and the chore is always the pet — fed, walked, and grinded by players who would rather be playing. Wiring the pet to the swing count deletes the chore and keeps the meaning: the companion's growth IS the record of everything you did together, because everything you did was thrusts. It also deletes a whole economy of exploits and purchases (there is no pet XP to sell, boost, or bot), a whole panel of UI (the companion panel shows ONE progress line — thrusts to next level — not two), and a whole category of player confusion ('why is my pet behind?') — your pet is never behind, because your pet is never anywhere but exactly where your own record put it. New companions from Slots 2 and 3 (Chapter 34) inherit the keeper's pet level the moment they grow: the level belongs to the bond the keeper has proven, not to the weeks a single creature has existed — a late companion is young in days and fully grown in attunement, which the fiction states outright: the Tree lends new branches the strength the keeper's record has already grown.
When they don't match — the refused equip, exactly
Because both gates read related numbers, a mismatch in this game is almost always a keeper reaching for a design drafted ahead of their record — the Workbench happily lets anyone DRAFT any tier (blueprints are imagination, and imagination is Chapter 37's whole economy) — and then trying to WIELD it early. The refusal is server-side, instant, and kind: the game shows its work instead of just saying no.

Build notes: the gating check is one server function and one number — Script 43 (weapon ownership) already owns the roster; add TierGate(player, tier) reading leaderstats Lifetime exactly as Scripts 19 and 35 do, with PetLevel(player) as a pure function of that same value (thresholds: 0 / 250 / 2,500 / 15,000 / 60,000 / 250,000). No new DataStore field exists for pet level — it is derived at read time, so it can never desync, be edited, or disagree with the count that made it. Chapter 12's test: draft a Tier 5 design on a fresh account (allowed), attempt to wield it (refused, card shows the unified gate), land the crossing thrust on a staged account (pet level and un-greying land in the same frame), and confirm no client call, purchase, or Workbench path equips above the gate.

39  Build the Tree in Studio — the Giant Pink Crystal Cherry Blossom Tree, step by step
This chapter builds ONE thing, completely: the Giant Pink Crystal Cherry Blossom Tree at the center of the floating island hometown (Chapter 3) — the same model Script 13 waits for by name. Follow the steps in order, in Roblox Studio, with the game open. Every size is in STUDS (Roblox's unit — one stud is roughly the width of a baseplate stud bump; a player character stands about 5 studs tall). At the end of this chapter the Tree stands about 120 studs tall over the island's Root Plaza, its roots grip the island rock, its canopy lights the town at night, and petals fall over the plaza forever — and Script 13's thrust offerings work on it with no code changes, because the model is named exactly what the code expects.

Before you start — settings and setup
Open the place in Studio. In the Explorer, make sure Workspace is visible. Turn on View → Properties and View → Output (you will set numbers in Properties all chapter).
Set the grid for building: Home tab → Snap to Grid ON, Move set to 1 stud, Rotate set to 15 degrees. Most Tree parts are placed by typing Position and Size numbers into Properties, not by dragging — typing is how the twists below stay even.
Decide the Tree's home position and write it down: the CENTER of the floating island, on the Root Plaza. Everything in this chapter is built around a single ground point called the Trunk Base: the top surface of the island at plaza level. Place a temporary Part (4 × 1 × 4, bright yellow, Name: DELETE_ME_LATER) with its top exactly at plaza level at the island's center — every height below is measured up from that top surface. Delete it in the final step.
The parts list — everything the Tree is made of
Build the whole Tree from these part families. Duplicate (Ctrl+D) inside each family instead of inserting new parts, so sizes and materials stay identical. Counts are for the finished Tree; build a few spares of the blossom clusters — duplicates are free until you press Play.

Color rule for the whole Tree, from Chapter 5: pink crystal is GLASS or SmoothPlastic in the petal pinks (#FF9ACB light, #E7549A hot) with a Neon core where it must glow; the trunk and branches are WOOD in dark walnut #4A3226. No other colors enter the Tree. If a part reads brown-pink or grey-pink in the plaza light, its color — not the lighting — is wrong.
Build it — numbered steps
Step 1 — Make the model and the folder structure (5 min). In Workspace, insert a Model, rename it GreatBlossomTree — exact capitals. Inside it insert three Folders: Trunk, Canopy, Roots. Every part you build goes into one of those folders (the TreeHitbox Part goes directly inside the Model, not in a folder). Select the Model and move it so the Trunk Base marker sits at its center: the Model's position is the island's center at plaza level.
Step 2 — Sink the root socket (10 min). The Tree does not sit ON the island; it grows THROUGH it. Under the plaza at the island's center, build a root socket: a cylinder hole visual made from 6 dark Wood wedges arranged in a ring, 16 studs across, angled inward and down, tops flush with the plaza stone. The trunk's lowest segment (Step 4) starts 4 studs BELOW plaza level inside this socket, so the Tree reads as planted, never placed. On the island's underside, this socket is where the roots of Step 3 emerge and grip the rock point.
Step 3 — Build the roots that grip the island (30 min). Build ONE main root, then duplicate it 6 times around the trunk. One main root: start at the socket at plaza level, run a Wedge 22 studs outward across the plaza edge of the socket, 5 wide and 4 tall, its top about 1 stud above the plaza at the trunk falling to flush at the tip — a surface root a player can walk over and sit on (these form the Root Plaza's natural benches and the offering circle's edge, Chapter 3). Continue the SAME root below: a second wedge from the socket angling down the island's underside, 18 studs long, ending in a point that bites into the island rock about two-thirds of the way to the island's tip. Duplicate around the trunk at 60-degree steps (Rotate snap 15° — use four clicks per root), varying each copy's length by 2–4 studs so the grip looks grown, not stamped. Add 12 small roots the same way at half scale between the mains, tops in the plaza soil ring. Test: from below the island, six root points visibly clutch the rock point; from the plaza, the roots read as one flared base, about 44 studs across.
Step 4 — Stack the trunk, with the twist (45 min). Insert a Cylinder Part (Part Type: Cylinder in Properties), Size 10 diameter — in Studio a cylinder's Size is (height, diameter, diameter); set Size to (6, 10, 10), Material Wood, Color #4A3226, Anchored on. Position its center 1 stud BELOW plaza level, so with its 6-stud height it spans from 4 studs below plaza level (inside the socket, where the roots meet it) to 2 studs above. Duplicate it upward 18 times: each copy sits directly on the one below (raise Position Y by 6), shrinks by 0.25 in diameter, and ROTATES 12 degrees around Y (Home → Rotate, or type Orientation Y +12 per segment). 18 segments × 6 studs = a trunk about 108 studs of stacked height including the buried socket section, with about 55 studs of clean trunk visible between the root flare and the first branches. The steady rotation is the twist — from the plaza the bark appears to spiral gently, and the crystal strips of Step 5 will follow the spiral. The top segment should be about 6 studs across. If the stack leans, a Position X/Z has drifted: every segment shares the Trunk Base X/Z exactly.
Step 5 — Lay the crystal core up the seams (20 min). The trunk is living wood grown around pink crystal (Chapter 3), and the crystal shows at the seams of the twist. On the front-facing seam of every OTHER trunk segment, place one crystal core strip: a Block 1.5 wide × 6 tall × 1 thick, set 0.5 studs proud of the trunk surface, rotated to match its segment's twist (same Orientation Y as the segment it sits on), Material Glass, Color #FF9ACB, Transparency 0.25. Work upward in a spiral, offsetting each strip about 30 degrees around the trunk from the one below, so a line of pink light climbs the trunk in a helix. 14 strips is the target. These strips are decoration over the wood — never replace a trunk segment with crystal; a glass trunk reads as a tower, not a tree.
Step 6 — Grow the branches (40 min). Branches start at about 55 studs up and occupy the top third of the trunk. Build one main branch: a Cylinder 22 long × 2.5 diameter, Wood #4A3226, laid near-horizontal (Orientation Z about 80 degrees, so it points outward with a slight rise). Attach its inner end INSIDE the trunk (overlap 3 studs — hidden joints need no joinery). Taper it by stacking a second, thinner cylinder (16 long × 1.5) continuing the same line, angled up 10 degrees more. Duplicate the main branch 9 times around the crown at varied heights (55–75 studs), lengths (18–26 studs), and outward angles — three low and wide, three mid, three high and steeper. On each main branch, add 2 secondary branches at half scale reaching up and out from its outer half. CanCollide OFF on every branch: players climb the Sky Obby, not the Tree, and a collidable canopy makes falling players snag in the crown.
Step 7 — Hang the blossom — crystal clusters (45 min). This is the step the Tree is judged by. Take one large blossom cluster (Ball, 12 diameter, squashed to about 0.7 height): Material Glass, Color #E7549A, Transparency 0.15. Inside it, centered, place one glow core (Ball, 3 diameter, Neon #FF9ACB) — the core is what the PointLights of Step 9 will appear to come from. Group cluster + core (Ctrl+G) and name the group Cluster_L. Now dress every branch: clusters sit at branch ENDS and along the outer half of each branch, never against the trunk — blossom belongs to the light, not the wood. Place 22 large clusters: the canopy they form should span about 90 studs across and roof the Root Plaza completely (stand at the plaza center and look up: no sky visible through the middle of the canopy; sky at the edges is correct). Fill gaps with 30 small clusters (SmoothPlastic #FF9ACB, 5–8 across) tucked between the large ones. Then set the crystal blossom shards: 26 Wedges of pink Glass sprouting where blossom meets wood — at the trunk fork, at branch joints, and out of the root flare — points up and outward, 4–9 studs tall. From the island's rim, the silhouette must read: dark twisted trunk, pink crystal crown, crystal teeth at every joint.
Step 8 — Place the TreeHitbox and the offering ground (10 min). Insert a Block Part directly inside the GreatBlossomTree Model. Rename it TreeHitbox — exact capitals. Size (14, 30, 14), Position centered on the trunk at 15 studs above plaza level (spanning plaza level to 30 up), Transparency 1, CanCollide OFF, CanQuery OFF, Anchored ON. This invisible box is what Script 13 measures the 16-stud offering range from and what thrusts connect with at the Tree. On the ground around it, the offering circle is plaza dressing: a flat ring (Cylinder, 32 diameter × 0.2 tall, stone) centered on the trunk — keep its edge inside the root flare so the circle and the roots read as one place.
Step 9 — Light the canopy — PointLights (20 min). The Tree is the town's lamp at night (Chapter 3), and it is lit from inside the blossom. Select 12 of the large clusters, spread evenly through the canopy (low, mid, and high; front, back, and sides). In each, insert a PointLight into the GLOW CORE part (not the cluster shell): Color #FF9ACB, Range 45, Brightness 2, Shadows OFF (shadow-casting lights are the expensive kind; twelve of them will tax a phone). Add 2 more PointLights in the trunk's crystal strips at mid-height, Range 30, Brightness 1.5, same color, so the helix glows as a line at night. Add ONE PointLight at the offering circle, Range 24, Brightness 1.5, Color #FF9ACB, inside an invisible part 6 studs above the circle — the plaza's hearth light. Budget rule: 15 PointLights total for the whole Tree, no more; if the night view is dim, raise Brightness on the canopy lights to 2.5 before adding a sixteenth light. Test: set Lighting ClockTime to 0 (midnight) and stand at the island's rim — the town should sit in pink light with the canopy as its source, and the trunk's crystal helix should be traceable from root to crown.
Step 10 — Make the petals fall — ParticleEmitters (20 min). Petal fall is two emitters, both in the Canopy folder. EMITTER A — the plaza fall: insert a Part (30 × 1 × 30, invisible, CanCollide OFF) centered 10 studs below the canopy's middle, about 70 studs above the plaza. Insert a ParticleEmitter into it. Set: Texture — a single soft pink petal (upload one pink petal image as a Decal in Creator Hub and use its asset ID; a plain pink rounded square also works at this size); Color — a ColorSequence from #FF9ACB to #E7549A; Size 0.6–1.0; Rate 20; Lifetime 6–9 seconds; Speed 3–5 (slow — petals drift, they do not rain); SpreadAngle 180 (falling in every downward direction); Acceleration (0, −1, 0) for a gentle settle; Rotation −90 to 90 with RotSpeed 30–60 so petals tumble; Transparency fading in at spawn and out before floor level (a NumberSequence: 1 → 0 at 20% → 0 → 1 at 100%) so no petal visibly pops at the ground. EMITTER B — the rim fall: a second invisible part (60 × 1 × 60) at the same height, Rate 8, Lifetime 10–14, Speed 2–4, drifting outward (add a slight outward Velocity spread) — these petals leave the island's edge and fall toward the clouds below, the view from the rim that sells the island's height. Performance rule: 28 particles per second across both emitters is the whole budget; on phone tests (Chapter 11) this reads as continuous fall. If a test device stutters, halve Emitter B first — never the plaza fall.
Step 11 — Finish — anchor audit, delete the marker, Play-test (15 min). Select the GreatBlossomTree Model. In Properties / with the Home tab: Anchor EVERY part (select all in the Model → Home → Anchor). Delete the DELETE_ME_LATER marker part. Press Play and run the chapter's test list below. Then set Lighting back to ClockTime 10 for the daytime save. Save (File → Publish) before leaving Studio — an unpublished Tree exists only on this computer.

40  The Gates — torii portals, the world-selection UI, and the swing-count ladder
Every gate in Jade Spirit is the same kind of object, and it works the same way everywhere: a Japanese TORII GATE standing as a portal — on the floating island's rim, at the ground shrines below, at every world's return point. Walk toward it and you see both worlds at once through its frame. Walk THROUGH it, and the game does not guess where you meant to go: a WORLD SELECTION UI opens, listing every world, each one gated by your SWING COUNT — your Lifetime thrusts (Chapter 4). Worlds you have earned glow open; worlds you have not yet earned show the exact count still to go. You pick; the gate takes you. That is the whole system, and this chapter designs all of it: what a gate looks like, what walking through it feels like, what the selection screen shows, what each world asks and holds, and how to build it in Studio on top of Scripts 19 and 20, whose thresholds this chapter uses unchanged.
The gate itself — design

Walking through — the portal transition
The crossing is a designed sequence of about two seconds, identical in shape at every gate, so players learn it once and trust it everywhere:


The world selection UI — design
The selection screen is a single panel, built for a phone held in two hands first (Chapter 11's rule) and readable at arm's length: it never shows more than the worlds, your count, and one decision.

The world list — gates, danger, and what each world holds
The ladder below is Script 19's own, unchanged: the three home worlds ask nothing, and the seven gated worlds ask the Lifetime counts the code already enforces. Zombie density, bosses, and rewards are stated per world so a keeper can read the whole game's shape off one screen at the gate. Densities are design targets for spawn tuning (Scripts 4, 29, and 31): zombies per active area at full server, rising with the ladder — the swing count buys danger, and danger pays.

Reading the ladder: the counts are Lifetime, so spending can never re-lock a world (Chapter 4), the pet level rises off the same count (Chapter 38), and the weapon tiers open in step — the keeper who can enter the Hollow Grove is, by the same record, a Pet Level 3 keeper who may wield Tier 3 designs. One number, read four ways, and the gate is where the player watches all four readings climb together: each card's progress bar is also their pet's and their next weapon tier's progress bar, and the gate UI says so in its footer — 'This count is also your pet's level and your weapon tier. One number drives everything.'

41  The apocalypse world — and King of the Hill at its heart
Through the gate (Chapter 40) is the second geography of Jade Spirit: the APOCALYPSE WORLD — the ruined ground far below the floating island, where the Thorn Sleep won. This chapter is its complete world bible: the environment, the rings, the landmarks, the safe pockets, the resources, the atmosphere — and at its center, the mode the whole world is built around. Read this plainly, because it shapes everything below: THE APOCALYPSE WORLD IS A KING OF THE HILL WORLD. It is not a sprawling open world to wander. It is one valley built around ONE HILL — one central point every zombie wave converges on and every keeper fights to hold. The ruins, rings, and landmarks exist to feed that hill: approaches to defend, pockets to recover in, nodes to dart out for between waves. One hill, one point, one fight the whole server shares.

Waves — the horde walks to the hill
Zombie waves are not spawned AT the hill; they MUSTER in the Deep Ruins fog (four muster grounds, one per road), a wave horn sounds across the valley, and the horde walks its road — past its shrine (which the defense meters of Script 31 govern), through the Ruins, up the Apron, and onto the terraces, converging on the summit from its ramp and the scramble slopes. On WINNING, this mode is honest, and Chapter 42 states it as law: there is no final victory over the Sleep in a single round — waves escalate until the hill falls and every keeper with it. 42  Difficulty is swings — and death is inevitable: the survival law
Two systems run every apocalypse round, and together they are the mode's identity. The first is DIFFICULTY, and in Jade Spirit difficulty is not a hidden stat — it is a number of SWINGS. Before a round, the player PICKS how many weapon swings it takes to free one zombie: Easy asks 1 swing, Normal 3, Hard 5, Nightmare 10, and Eternal 20. Because every connecting swing is a counted thrust (Chapter 4), the choice is self-paying with no multiplier trickery: a Nightmare zombie takes ten swings and therefore EARNS ten counted swings — ten times the progression of the same zombie on Easy — while standing in front of you ten times as long, which is how the horde gets you. The second system is the round's ending, and it is guaranteed: INEVITABLE DEATH SURVIVAL. Waves escalate endlessly (below) until every keeper is overwhelmed. There is no winning a round — there is only lasting longer, holding more, and banking everything you earned, because dying banks your count: nothing a keeper earned in the apocalypse is ever lost to their fall.
The difficulty selector — UI

The swings-to-free table — difficulty, exactly
A zombie's WARD is its health, set in damage points as a multiple of the REFERENCE SWING — the starting swing power of 25 (Chapter 43). Target swings below are therefore exact at starting power: ward ÷ 25. As a keeper's swing power grows (Chapter 43, capped), the same ward takes fewer, stronger swings — that reduction is the growth loop's visible payoff, and the selector card recomputes it (above). Bosses carry wards as multiples of the round's zombie ward, so difficulty scales them by the same choice.


Escalation — the endless curve
Waves are numbered from 1, forever. Each wave is built from the round's difficulty ward and three growth rules, applied per wave and never capped — the curve is DESIGNED to overtake any party eventually; that overtaking is the mode (below). Design targets for a full server in the Hollow Grove (Chapter 41); other worlds shift the base by their danger (Chapter 40).

The escalation's fairness rules: growth is announced (the wave banner shows count, and the HUD shows the ward as 'swings per zombie at your power' so the party watches its own number climb); nothing spawns inside the Apron without walking its road from a muster ground; and the lull never falls below 30 seconds — even the end comes with breath between its waves, because a death you can see coming is drama and a death from nowhere is a bug report.
The death sequence — dramatic, and rewarding
A keeper's fall is staged in five beats over about eight seconds. It is never a screen slam, never a mockery, and never framed with the word death inside the game's fiction for its youngest keepers: on screen it is THE FALL — the Sleep takes you, standing, the way it took the Hollow (Chapter 1) — and the game treats it as the round's most honorable moment, because it is the one every round is guaranteed to contain.

The round summary and the leaderboard — lasting longer is the record

Dying banks your count — the progression law
State the wiring exactly, because players must be able to trust it before their first fall: counted swings are credited by Script 13 AT THE MOMENT THEY LAND, all round long — the fall does not carry the count home in a bag that can spill. What the death sequence's banking beat adds is a FLUSH: the fall triggers an immediate save of the keeper's record (Lifetime, Spend Balance, and Chapter 43's account damage) rather than waiting for the economy's 30-second cycle (Script 13), and the summary card is drawn from the SAVED record — the number it shows is the number in the DataStore, not a promise. So the law can be stated in one line on the selector, the HUD, and the summary alike: EVERY SWING YOU LAND IS YOURS FOREVER, INCLUDING THE LAST ONE. The apocalypse's bargain is therefore the fairest in the game: it will take your run, your hill, and eventually your standing body — and it cannot touch a single number you earned. Players who understand that bargain take braver last stands, and braver last stands are the content this mode exists to produce. Build note: the flush-on-fall must ride Chapter 14's receipt and save discipline exactly (a failed flush retries on the wake, shows 'banking…' honestly until it lands, and never displays a banked number it has not confirmed) — a banking screen that lies once would poison the mode's whole thesis.

43  One number — damage dealt IS swing power IS your account
Jade Spirit has no damage stat. It has DAMAGE DEALT — a single account total, kept beside your counts — and that total IS your swing power, read through one curve. Every point of damage you have ever dealt to a zombie, a husk, or a boss is recorded on your account; your account reads that record back as strength: the more damage you have dealt, the harder every swing lands, which deals more damage, which makes the next swing harder. One number, three readings — damage dealt = swing power = account progression — and no other damage number exists anywhere: not on the weapon (weapons have designs and tiers, Chapter 38, never damage stats), not on the pet (pet level is the swing count, Chapter 38), not in the shop (Chapter 6 sells no power, and now there is not even a power-shaped hole for a shop to fill).
The loop, stated exactly

The curve — swing power from account damage
SWING POWER = 25 + 25 × √(AccountDamage ÷ 100,000), rounded DOWN to a whole number, CAPPED at 125. The square root is the design: power grows fast while you are new (the first 100,000 damage doubles your swing from 25 to 50), then stretches into a long mastery climb, and the cap at five times starting power is a wall, not a suggestion — at 1,600,000 lifetime damage a keeper's swing is 125 and the loop's power story is complete; damage dealt beyond the cap still records, still ranks, and still feeds frees against wards (Chapter 42), but power itself has a ceiling every account can actually reach.




44  The look starts legendary — customization is identity, not stats
This chapter states the game's customization philosophy as law, and updates the four base characters to match it. THE PRINCIPLE: a default character in Jade Spirit looks like LEVEL 100 — maxed out, epic, the character on the box — from the very first minute. New players do not choose between weak-looking starters and dream of someday looking powerful; the FIRST screen of character options is the aspirational screen. And what customization beyond the base unlocks is not strength at all: it is PERSONAL PREFERENCE. Deep customization is where a keeper stops wearing the legend and starts expressing themselves — their character, their pet, their weapon, rebuilt around who they are. Customization is identity. It has never been stats, and this chapter separates the two so completely that no future system can confuse them again.

46  The Colosseum — pay-to-view live Last Man Standing
The Colosseum is the game's stage: a spectator arena where up to eight contestants fight an all-or-nothing Last Man Standing match on a King of the Hill zombie apocalypse floor (Chapters 41–43, staged as a show) — while everyone else WATCHES LIVE, and live costs. Spectating a live match is a pay-to-view product, sold in Robux through Roblox's own purchase prompts and this package's existing receipt pipeline (Chapters 6 and 14). The free tier is real but delayed: the full match replay, free, after the match ends. This chapter designs the arena, the contest, the tickets, what a ticket actually buys, how the money splits, and the two scripts that run it — and it states the three laws that keep a pay-to-view show honest in a game built for younger players first.

The arena — a hill with an audience
Build the Colosseum as its own island in the same place, reached by its gate (Chapter 40): a circular stone-and-timber arena whose floor is the apocalypse valley in miniature — one central HILL (Chapter 41's summit and control circle, at show scale), four zombie gates in the floor wall, cracked grey earth and fog pockets inside the wall, and the island in the sky visible above the rim, because even here home is up. Around and above the floor, the STANDS: three rising tiers of benches behind a blossom-light curtain wall that spectators cannot cross and contestants cannot leave — the same light-curtain law as the gates (Chapter 3), doing crowd control. Spectators are bodies in seats, never bodies on the floor.

Contestant entry — buy in, or qualify
Fighting is never pay-to-view and never Robux: entry is earned currency or earned qualification, and brackets keep it fair. A match takes a maximum of 8 contestants (the server holds 12 — the rest of the server is the crowd) and starts at a minimum of 4. Entry runs in two brackets by Chapter 38's tiers — Grove Bracket (Tiers 1–3) and Eternal Bracket (Tiers 4–5) — so a new keeper's first match is against their own ladder, not against an Eternal Partner.

Last Man Standing — the rules of the match

All-or-nothing stakes — winner takes all
The pool is the sum of the buy-ins, escrowed by Script 49 the moment each contestant enters, visible on the live board from the lobby onward — a spectator can always see exactly what the last keeper standing will take. The winner receives the whole pool as Bonus thrusts through Script 13 (which credits Spend Balance only, in its own clamped chunks, so a large pool pays out in full without ever touching Lifetime). Every other contestant receives nothing from the pool: not a refund, not a share, not a parting gift. Their swings during the match still counted — damage dealt is still swing power (Chapter 43), and a loser's match is still progression. What they lost is only what they staked. That sentence is printed on the entry card, before the buy-in button, in the same size as the button.
Pay-to-view — live costs, the replay is free
A live match can also be followed, free and delayed, on the plaza board at home: the hill holder, the standing count, and the pool, as text — the score, never the show. The SHOW — being in the stands while it happens, with the cameras in your hands — is the product. This is the game's one pay-to-view offer, and its tiers are drawn so the free tier is a complete experience of a finished match, and the paid tier is the live moment itself:

What a live ticket actually buys — the premium cameras

Predictions — free cheers, never bets
Every spectator — paid live or watching the delayed board — may pick one contestant to win, free, from the lobby until Wave 3 begins (Script 49 locks picks then, server-side). A correct pick earns the Oracle spectator title track and a fixed 25 Bonus thrusts — a thank-you for watching closely, identical for every correct pick, funded by the game and never by other spectators. Nothing is staked, so nothing can be lost, and no pick can be bought, boosted, or changed after the lock. Contestants may not pick their own match. This system is a cheer with a memory, and it stays one: it is named PREDICTIONS everywhere it appears, never odds, never betting, never wagers.
How to buy a ticket — the purchase flow
Tickets are bought the Roblox way, and only the Roblox way: no external store, no codes, no trading. (1) At the ticket gate in the Colosseum lobby, or from the plaza board's WATCH LIVE button at home, the spectator opens the ticket card (Script 50). (2) The card shows the three live tiers with Robux prices, the match's announced difficulty and pool, and — in the same size type — the free alternative: 'Or watch the full replay, free, when the match ends.' (3) Tapping a tier opens Roblox's own purchase prompt (MarketplaceService) — the game never sees, asks for, or handles payment details. (4) The purchase completes through Script 10's ProcessReceipt: the receipt is recorded once in the persistent PurchaseId ledger (Chapter 14), routed to Script 49's JadeColosseumGrantTicket, and the entitlement lands server-side. (5) The spectator taps ENTER THE STANDS; Script 49 re-checks the entitlement on the server and only then teleports them in. A client that claims to hold a ticket it never bought gets the ticket card again, politely, and nothing else. The Season Pass (a Game Pass) is checked with UserOwnsGamePassAsync and cached per session by Script 49. Refunds and chargebacks are Roblox's process, never the game's: if Roblox reverses a purchase, the entitlement it bought simply stops validating.
The revenue split — where a ticket's Robux goes
Published on the ticket card, in full, because spectators are funding the show and deserve to see the split. Roblox's marketplace fee comes first — 30% of every sale, the platform's standard cut (Chapter 6; re-verify in Creator Hub at publish). What remains is the game's net, and the net splits two ways:

The Prize Conversion, stated once and used everywhere: for each match, Script 49 totals the prize-fund allocation from that match's ticket sales (in Robux, net as above) and converts it at 10 Bonus thrusts per 1 Robux, added to the winner's pool payout on top of the buy-ins. A sold-out stand therefore pays the winner measurably more than an empty one — the contestants can see the crowd, the crowd can see the pool, and both sides of the curtain are watching the same number. Contestants receive Spend Balance and titles, never Robux (Law 2): the Robux itself never leaves the game account, because on Roblox it cannot — any design that promises players Robux prizes is promising something the platform does not let a game do.

The loyalty loop — spend in the Vault, watch in the stands
Whatever you spend in the Sales Vault is given back as Colosseum view time. Not points toward a discount, not a raffle entry: the same value, returned in the game's other currency of attention — minutes, live, in the stands. The rule is one line, printed in the Vault and at the ticket gate alike: 1 ROBUX SPENT IN THE VAULT = 1 MINUTE OF LIVE COLOSSEUM VIEW TIME. Buy the $0.99 skin (80 Robux) and you hold 80 minutes — enough, at the calibrated match lengths below, for seven standard matches with minutes to spare. Buy nothing ever, and the free delayed replay (Chapter 46) still shows you every match in full. The loop never gates the story; it rewards the spending that already happened.

Why the loop works — both directions, stated plainly
Vault → Colosseum: every purchase manufactures an audience member. A keeper who came to buy a skin leaves holding 80 minutes that are only spendable watching other keepers fight — so matches get crowds, crowds make the pool's prize conversion grow (Chapter 46), and a bigger announced pool draws contestants. Colosseum → Vault: the stands are the skin catalogue's best room. Spectators spend matches watching contestants' weapons at player-cam distance — every skin in the lineup, worn in a real fight, under arena light — and the Vault is one gate away when the match ends; champions' skins get a 'worn by the winner' card in the Vault for a week (a display fact, server-recorded, never a discount claim). Neither direction nags: the Vault never interrupts a match, the stands never open a shop prompt, and the two panels simply keep showing each other in the balance strip. The loop is two doors and a corridor, walked voluntarily, in both directions, forever.
Calibration — the spend-to-view ratio, measured against the game's own numbers
The ratio is 1:1 because every other candidate hid a conversion. 1 Robux spent = 1 View Credit = 1 minute of standard-rate live viewing needs no exchange table, no rounding rule, and no fine print — a player can check it against any price in the game with one glance. What follows is that one ratio, applied to the package's actual prices and actual match structure. Chapter 49's ledger labels every number below: prices and cadences are SPECIFIED (design choices, set deliberately), and every total beside them is MEASURED (counted from the code, or arithmetic on the specified values — the working is shown).

Per dollar, using the package's own anchor: the skin is priced at the $0.99 tier — 80 Robux — so a $0.99 Vault purchase banks exactly 80 view minutes. There is no per-dollar table beyond that anchor, because Robux reaches accounts by many routes (bundles, Premium, gifts) at many effective prices; the honest unit is the Robux spent in the Vault, and the ratio is stated in Robux.
Round lengths — what a minute of credit actually buys, per mode

Popularity — star matches are worth more view time
View Credit burns at 1 credit per minute, times the match's popularity multiplier. A star's match is worth more of your banked time because it is scarcer — there is one reigning top of the Value board (Chapter 48), and a server of twelve can only stage so many matches around them. The multiplier is set by Script 49 at the start whistle, from counted facts on Script 53's Character Value board — who is actually fighting — never from a hand-picked list, never from anything a player can buy, and it NEVER applies to Robux tickets: a 49-Robux ticket admits its holder to a Marquee final at the same price as a quiet Tuesday match. Only loyalty credit, which cost the game nothing to issue, is weighted.

The balance formula — why the economy cannot inflate
Supply: total View Credit issued = total Robux spent in the Vault (1:1, from receipts; Script 51). Sink: total credit burned = live minutes watched × popularity multiplier (Script 49). Three guardrails keep supply and sink in their lanes. (1) The 600-minute personal cap bounds outstanding liability per player — the worst case is always countable: players × 600. (2) Credit is time, not purchasing power: it buys nothing but presence at a show whose marginal cost is a seat in an already-running server, so an unspent balance is not a debt the economy must honor in goods. (3) The popularity multiplier makes the scarcest content consume credit fastest, so a single skin cannot camp every star match of a season: at Marquee rate, the season's biggest matches cost the bank at double speed, exactly as their scarcity says they should. If the duration log (median of 20) ever shows the anchor has drifted by more than 2 minutes, the recalibration note prints on the ticket card before the next match is sold — the ratio players bought under is the ratio they are charged under, changed only in daylight, between matches, never during one.

49  The Measurement Ledger — every number, labelled
This ledger exists because of one rule: never estimate, and never present a design decision as a measurement. Every canon number in this package carries one of two labels. SPECIFIED means a deliberate design choice — someone chose it, it is marked as chosen, and it stands until a designer changes it on purpose. MEASURED means the value was obtained by counting, by reading the source it lives in, or by arithmetic on specified values — and the method is stated beside it, so anyone can re-derive it. One honesty note governs the whole ledger: this game has not launched, so NO number in this package comes from live play. Anything that sounds like a playtest result — a match length, a survival time — is either a specified design target or an arithmetic derivation labelled as such, and Chapter 50's tuning system exists precisely to replace those anchors with real measurements once real players provide them.
Counts — measured by counting

Combat and economy — the specified core, the derived ceilings

Prices and ratios — specified prices, measured arithmetic

Dimensions, speeds, and timers not listed individually — stud sizes in build tables, zombie speeds in Chapter 42's curve, lull lengths of 45–75 s, scope and range figures in Chapter 36 — are uniformly SPECIFIED: build instructions and design choices, every one, with no exceptions smuggled in as observations. If a future edition of this package ever prints a number it calls measured from play, Chapter 50's logs are the only permitted source, and the log's date range must print beside it.

50  Adaptive Balancing — the game tunes itself, inside caps
Every number in this package starts as a SPECIFIED design value (Chapter 49). From the first real match onward, the game measures reality against those values and adjusts — itself, automatically, in small steps, inside hard caps, and never across the lines this chapter names. The system is Script 55, and its whole philosophy fits in one sentence: the game may tune how the horde feels and how rewards flow, because those were always estimates wearing specified labels — and it may never touch a promise, because promises were never estimates.
What is measured — the metric record

What adjusts — the tuned values, their thresholds, and their caps

The never list — what the game may not tune, at any signal strength
Base damage 25. Every price (skins 80, tickets 49/99/299, passes, buy-ins). The gate ladder. Pet Level and tier thresholds. The 1:1 view-credit ratio and the 600 cap. The popularity multipliers. The Character Value weights. The UserId locks, and everything about Oakley's Singular. The cosmetic law. Chapter 49's ledger states why in one line: these are promises and identities, not estimates — a system that retunes its promises is not balancing, it is moving the goalposts, and players can tell. Script 55 contains no code path to any of them; adding one means editing the file by hand, in daylight, as a design change with a name on it.
When and how an adjustment lands
A tuning pass runs every 5 minutes of server time and acts only when 20 fresh rounds are banked AND no Colosseum match is live (Script 49's phase gate) — numbers change between matches, never during one, and at most one step per value per pass. Every pass, including the passes that change nothing, is written to the Tuning DataStore and printed to the server log with its median and its reasoning (Script 55's warn line), and the current factors ride Script 55's broadcast to the dashboard board. A bad step is therefore visible, dated, and reversible: next pass can step back, and Taylor can pin any factor by editing CAPS in Script 55 — a pin is a design act and outranks the tuner permanently.

51  The Business Model — freemium, the flywheel, and the loop
This chapter assembles the whole business from parts this package already built and audited — no borrowed claims, no market statistics, no other game's numbers. Every price below is a specified price from Chapters 6, 31, 46, or 47; every net figure is arithmetic on Roblox's 30% marketplace fee (Chapter 6, re-verify at publish); every scenario is labelled a scenario, with its assumptions stated, per Chapter 49's ledger rules. Where a familiar industry mechanism does not fit this game's own systems, the chapter says so and uses the system's own version instead.
Freemium and dual currency — the foundation
The game is free to play, completely: every world, the First Choice, King of the Hill, the full delayed Colosseum replay, and progression to Eternal Partner cost nothing. Two currencies run it, and they never mix. SWINGS (Shards, Blooms, and the thrust counts of Script 13) are earned by play, at Chapter 6's audited faucet ceilings, and buy in-game things — seeds, garden goods, the Thrust Shop's catalogue, Colosseum buy-ins. ROBUX is purchased, and buys cosmetics and views only: skins, passes, kimonos, effects, and live tickets. The wall between them is the business model's first law, enforced in code (Chapter 14): no Robux product grants power, progression, or a count; no earned currency is sold. Free players are not a funnel's raw material here — they are the contestants, the crowds, and the creators the paying systems need to exist at all.

Net figures are Robux arithmetic before Roblox's whole-Robux crediting and DevEx conversion (Chapter 6's terms, re-verified at publish); they are unit economics, not income. Nothing in this table is a projection.
The creator flywheel — players make the content that makes the players
Jade Spirit's content engine is its players. The Workbench (Chapter 28) designs characters, masks, weapons, and wings; World 1's building plots (Chapter 3) hold player-built homes; the Showcase (Chapter 33) stages player designs; creativity contests (Chapter 37) judge them weekly on published criteria; and the Colosseum (Chapter 46) turns the best fighters into watched content. Each turn of the wheel feeds the next, and every incentive on it is one the package already pays — in titles, Spend Balance, and making-capacity, never in power and never in Robux (a game cannot pay its players Robux; the flywheel pays in standing, which Chapter 48 made countable):

The engagement loop — hangout, stage, and core game

Unit economics — worked scenarios, labelled as scenarios
A scenario is arithmetic with its assumptions printed on it; it is not a forecast, and Chapter 49's rules forbid dressing it as one. Scenario A — one full Colosseum match (assumptions stated: 8 contestants, the server's remaining 4 seats filled by live spectators — 2 on Match Tickets, 1 on a Day Pass already purchased, 1 watching on View Credit): ticket revenue counted for this match = 2 × 49 = 98 Robux gross → 68.6 net → 34.3 to the prize & show fund → at Chapter 46's conversion, +343 Bonus thrusts added to a winner's pool of 8 buy-ins (Grove bracket: 8 × 250 = 2,000 Spend escrowed). The game's retained share of the match's ticket sales is 34.3 Robux; the credit viewer cost the game no Robux and burned 11 anchor-minutes × the match's popularity rate from a bank a Vault purchase created. Scenario B — one skin sale: 80 gross → 56 net to the game, and an 80-minute view-credit liability issued against it — a liability denominated in seat-time inside servers that are already running, redeemable only as presence, capped at 600 per player (Chapter 47). The model's discipline is that both scenarios close with the same sentence: the earned economy's ceilings (Chapter 6) were never touched, no power was sold, and the numbers a reader cannot re-derive from a stated price and a stated assumption do not appear.
What deliberately does NOT appear in this model, and why: rarity in Jade Spirit is set by the catalogue's own five tiers and counted ownership (Chapter 48) — measured inside the game, from the game's records. Systems from outside this game were offered as rarity inputs during design and declined on the page here: a number imported from another project would arrive with no instrument in this game able to verify it, and Chapter 49's ledger has no row for numbers like that. The business runs on its own data or it does not run.

53  The Code Gates — the game is the laboratory
This chapter changes what a gate IS. Until now every gate in this package asked one question — how large is your Lifetime count (Chapter 40, Script 19)? A code-gate asks a harder, more interesting question: it runs Taylor's own mathematics — the G48 present fixed point, the H14 / CORE door system, the filed refusal codec, the thermal model — on the player's live play, and the answer the mathematics returns is the gate's decision. The game stops being a picture of his work and becomes an execution environment for it: a laboratory where the instruments are his code, the specimens are live players, and every verdict is measured and written down.

The live data pipeline — production data, not test data
A code-gate is only as honest as its inputs, and its inputs are the live game. Script 58 (CodeGate) installs a single event bus — the BindableEvent JadeLiveEvent in ServerScriptService — and taps the game's real traffic at its sources. Nothing is simulated: the events below are the same events the rest of the game already runs on.

Each event lands in a per-player ring buffer — the last 120 events, newest last — which is the only history a module may read. The ring is deliberately small: a gate judges the player's present, not their biography, and a bounded buffer cannot grow into a lag source. Events are validated on arrival (kind is a string, player is live and in-game); an event that fails validation is re-queued once, and an event that fails twice is quarantined — copied to the ledger's quarantine list, never replayed into a gate, never silently dropped. The pipeline repairs itself around bad data instead of stopping on it.
The code-gate interface — how Taylor's code plugs in
A module is one ModuleScript in ServerScriptService → CodeGateModules, returning one table. That is the whole contract — anything Taylor can write as a function of the snapshot can drive a gate, in any of his frameworks, without touching the engine:

Binding is physical and visible in Studio: a gate is a Part named CodeGate_<Key> carrying three attributes — GateModule (the module's Id), GateMode (SHADOW or ARMED), and FallbackRequired (the classic Lifetime number). Its destination is Spawn_<Key>, exactly as in Chapter 40. Any existing Chapter 40 gate can become a code-gate by renaming its pad and setting the attributes; no other system notices the difference.
Shadow first, armed second — how a module earns a live gate
No module touches a player on its first day. In SHADOW mode the gate obeys its classic rule — the player crosses or not by the FallbackRequired count — while the module evaluates the same live moment and logs the verdict it WOULD have given. Shadow verdicts cost the player nothing and teach the laboratory everything: agreement rate with the classic rule, refusal rate, residual distribution, fault count. The owner arms a gate per pad (GateMode = ARMED) only after its shadow record reads clean in the ledger, and disarming is the same one attribute. A module version bump returns its gates to shadow in the owner's checklist — new code re-earns trust, it does not inherit it.
The four reference gates — his frameworks, running
Four reference modules ship with this chapter, each a real port of its source system's stated rules — the formulas below are the sources' own, cited to their documents in this package's evidence, and the Luau in this chapter implements exactly them and no more.

The gate card — players watch the code judge them
Script 59 draws the verdict card after every approach: the gate's name, the module's name, ADMITTED / REPAIRED — ADMITTED / REFUSED, the module's own reason in plain words, and the measured residual it decided by. This is the laboratory made visible — and it is the game's best teaching surface: a refused keeper sees the number, the rule, and what to change (play the window again, bring a different pair, rest the core), which makes every refusal a puzzle with a published solution instead of a wall.
Self-healing — the gates repair themselves, the game never stops
Production code fails; a children's game may not. The recovery design has one axiom: a broken module degrades its gate to the classic rule, never the game to a broken state. Script 58 enforces it at the point of failure, and Script 60 (JadeWatchdog) supervises everything around it:

Alerts are records, not interruptions: every intervention is written to the ledger and printed to the server log under the [WATCHDOG] tag, which Creator Hub surfaces after the session — Taylor reads the game's repair history the way he reads any lab notebook, after the fact, with the game never having asked a player to wait for it. The watchdog's vocabulary is deliberately tiny — move, reset, fall back, record. It never touches currency, Lifetime, damage, prices, or saved data, and it cannot kick or ban: a repair system with no weapons cannot become an incident.
The learning loop — usage makes the gates smarter, inside fences
Every verdict makes the next verdict better — measurably, reversibly, and only inside bounds the owner set in code. The loop has four stages, all in Script 58, all logged:

What improves, concretely: gate bands tighten toward the population that actually plays (the G48 band finds the swing cadence real keepers sustain; the Soak Gate's band finds the session rhythm of real play); generation gets better raw material (door pairs and frame faults are drawn from distributions the ledger actually observed); and the owner's picture sharpens — residual histograms per module per version are the tuning evidence Chapter 50 always wanted. What can NEVER be learned away: the fences. Calibration moves only numbers a module itself declares, inside its own hard bounds; it holds no handle on damage (25), any price, any other system's thresholds, the UserId locks, or the cosmetic law — Chapter 50's never-list, enforced here by the same construction as everywhere: the capability is not in the room. And the guardrail with no exceptions: a candidate that would make any measured outcome worse is not adopted, and an adoption that degrades is rolled back — the system is allowed to stay the same, never to get worse.
The laboratory workflow — Taylor's bench, in the game
This is what the platform is FOR. The loop Taylor already runs on paper — formalize, verify, measure — now runs where players live: (1) write the framework as a ModuleScript (port the rule, cite the source in its header, declare its bounds); (2) drop it in CodeGateModules and bind one gate in SHADOW; (3) play — his own sessions and every live server generate the verdict stream; (4) read the ledger (Studio: Script 58's _G.JadeGateLedgerDump(); live: the CodeGateLedger_v1 DataStore, one key per day, capped at 900 entries); (5) revise the module, bump Version, re-shadow, re-arm. A hypothesis about G48's thermal band stops being a spreadsheet claim and becomes a measured property of a thousand real crossings. The game is the laboratory; the ledger is its notebook; the players, playing, are the experiment running.

SANCTUARY RULES — World 1 is HOME:  Safe world, build world, NO PvP — and a world in the SKY: the island floats above the apocalypse, so safety here is geography, not just rules; the horde below cannot climb to a home that hangs over the clouds. Players cannot fight each other here — not by spear, not by Daemon, not by any system. No Hollow skeletons, no Thorn Husks, and no wave ever spawns inside the sanctuary or follows a player into it. Combat — the zombie and skeleton waves, husk-freeing, the Arena — happens in other zones and worlds, reached through the torii gates (Chapter 40). World 1 is where keepers prepare for that fight and come home from it: customize at the Workbench, build on their plots, shop, group up, and rest. The World Tree stands here protected — it cannot be damaged at home, ever.

-- Jade Spirit | 13_BlossomTree.server.lua
-- Location: ServerScriptService > insert Script, rename it BlossomTree
-- What it does: the Great Blossom Tree (Chapter 16) AND the game's
-- central thrust counter. The Tree stands at the centre of the Grove;
-- hitting it bursts petals and shimmers its crystals. Every
-- connecting spear thrust anywhere -- Tree, Thorn Husk, or Blossom
-- Arena opponent -- is reported here by Script 2 and counted ONCE,
-- under the PLAYER.
--
-- ============================================================
-- THE COUNT BELONGS TO THE PLAYER, NEVER THE WEAPON
-- ============================================================
-- * Personal counts are stored under "player_<UserId>" and global
--   totals under one shared key. Nothing anywhere is keyed by Tool,
--   skin, or variant: a player who swaps from the Wood spear to
--   the Golden skin mid-session keeps one continuous count, because
--   the counting function below receives a Player and a source --
--   it is never even told which weapon thrust.
-- * The equipped variant IS recorded, as cosmetic metadata in the
--   same record (WeaponVariant), because it is nice to know. It is
--   written on save from the player's SpearVariant attribute and
--   read by NOTHING that counts, ranks, pays, or unlocks.
-- * _G.JadeCountThrust is server-only (clients share no _G with the
--   server) and still re-validates: the source must be one of the
--   three real ones, the player must be alive and -- for Tree and
--   Arena sources -- genuinely standing where that source lives,
--   and counted thrusts are rate-capped per player. Script 2's
--   report is a claim; this function is the audit.
-- ============================================================
--
-- ============================================================
-- TWO COUNTS, TWO INDEPENDENT VALUES, BOTH THE PLAYER'S
-- ============================================================
-- * LIFETIME is the record: total connecting thrusts ever. It
--   only ever goes UP. It unlocks zones, sets ranks and titles,
--   grows the Susanoo, and feeds achievements. Nothing spends
--   it, nothing refunds it, nothing resets it.
-- * SPEND BALANCE is the wallet: a SEPARATE stored value. Each
--   counted thrust credits it by the same factor that credits
--   Lifetime, and bonus grants credit it alone -- but from that
--   moment the two values live apart. Spending (the Thrust Shop)
--   subtracts from Spend Balance ONLY.
-- * They are stored as two independent fields in the player's
--   record -- Spend Balance is NOT computed from Lifetime. Worked
--   example: a player at Lifetime 1,000 / Spend 1,000 buys a
--   300-thrust cosmetic. Spend becomes 700. Lifetime stays 1,000:
--   the zone gate that opened at 1,000 stays open, the rank the
--   1,000 earned stays earned. They land 10 more thrusts:
--   Lifetime 1,010, Spend 710. Two numbers, two jobs, no leakage.
-- * BOTH counts are pinned to the PLAYER (key "player_<UserId>").
--   Neither is tied to a weapon, a character, a Daemon pet, or
--   an appearance: swap spears, swap Daemons, rebuild a look at
--   the Workbench -- both counts follow the player, permanently.
-- ============================================================
